DriftScope
text:
How to read this book
If you are…

new to oceanography — start with Chapter 5 and read Physics in order. The math is undergraduate-level vector calculus; we build intuition before formalism.
new to the codebase but comfortable with the physics — skim Physics, then go to Modules (Chapter 16) for the file-by-file reference, then Tutorials to run things.
here to extend the project — read the relevant Physics chapter, the matching module reference, then Chapter 23 which walks through adding a new term to Eq. 1 end-to-end.
here to evaluate the model — Validation lives in the drifter comparison tutorial and the drifter-validation Python scripts under scripts/.

title: DriftScope
text:
What this book is not

Not a textbook on physical oceanography. We assume comfort with \(\mathbf{u} = (u, v)\), partial derivatives, and the idea of a velocity field. Anything beyond that we explain when it comes up.
Not API documentation. Every public function in driftscope/ has a docstring; this book teaches you how the pieces fit, not the signature of every helper.
Not exhaustive. We trade completeness for a clear path. Edges — model internals, second-order effects, alternative algorithms — get a footnote pointing to the relevant paper or commit.

title: DriftScope
text:
Conventions

File references look like driftscope/simulate.py:165 — line numbers are stable to within a few lines if the file has been edited since the book was written.
Code blocks beginning with python are runnable; you can copy-paste them into a notebook in the project root after conda activate driftscope.
Callouts:

Why — a design decision worth understanding.
Caveat — a place the model lies, or where the data is thinner than it looks.
Try it — small exercise. Five-to-fifteen minutes.

Acknowledgments
This project exists because of decades of public ocean data and open-source infrastructure. Major debts: the Copernicus Marine Service for currents and SST; ECMWF and the Climate Data Store for ERA5; the OSU TPXO project for tides; NOAA AOML for the Global Drifter Program; the OceanParcels team for the Lagrangian framework the simulation runs on.
The structural inspiration is Lenain et al. (2026)’s GOFLOW: a single physics equation, one term at a time, validated against drifters. We follow the same recipe at coarser resolution.




Lenain, L. et al. (2026). GOFLOW: Geostationary ocean flow. Nature Geoscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-01943-0

3 Setup
This chapter gets you from a clean machine to “I can run a simulation.” Allow ~15 min if you already have conda; ~30 min from scratch.

title: 2  Setup
text:
3.1 Prerequisites
You need:

Python 3.11 via Miniconda or Mambaforge. The project pins parcels, copernicusmarine, and pyTMD versions that don’t always coexist nicely with system Python; conda gives us isolation.
Git to clone the repo.
About 5 GB of disk for the conda environment, plus 1–2 GB for cached data per region/month you simulate.
Free accounts at:

Copernicus Marine — for currents (CMEMS) and SST (OSTIA).
Climate Data Store — for ERA5 waves and winds.
TPXO registration (optional) — if you want tides. Skip if you only care about currents.

title: 2  Setup
text:
3.2 Clone and create the environment
git clone <repo-url> sundarban
cd sundarban
conda env create -f environment.yml      # ~3 min on a warm conda cache
conda activate driftscope
The environment file is at environment.yml. Key pinned packages:

parcels >= 3.0 — the Lagrangian framework
copernicusmarine >= 2.0 — CMEMS API client
cdsapi — ERA5 client
pytmd >= 3.0 — tides
xarray + netcdf4 + zarr — data plumbing
streamlit + pydeck + folium — dashboard







Tip



Why conda not pip? Several of these (parcels, pytmd, rioxarray, cartopy) have C/Fortran extensions whose binary wheels on PyPI lag conda-forge. On Linux pip will mostly work but on macOS/Windows the binary mismatch story is painful enough that we standardize on conda.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
4 Quickstart
Five commands. End-to-end. The point is to confirm the stack works on your machine before you read about why it works.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
4.1 The five commands
# 1) Currents for the default region (Sundarbans, last 14 days)
python -m driftscope.fetch

# 2) Run a 500-particle, 10-day simulation
python -m driftscope.simulate

# 3) Render a quick-look plot
python -c "
from pathlib import Path
import xarray as xr, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from driftscope.viz import load_trajectories, traj_to_dataframe

ds = load_trajectories(sorted(Path('data/trajectories').glob('*.zarr'))[-1])
df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
plt.scatter(df.lon, df.lat, s=1, c=df.time.astype('int64'),
            cmap='magma', alpha=0.4)
plt.savefig('data/quickstart_traj.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print('saved data/quickstart_traj.png')
"

# 4) (Optional) Launch the interactive dashboard
streamlit run app.py
If data/quickstart_traj.png shows a plume of dots seeded near the Sundarbans coast and spreading offshore, you have a working install.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
4.2 What just happened
Let’s unpack each step.

4.2.1 Step 1 — fetch currents
python -m driftscope.fetch resolves to driftscope/fetch.py’s main(). It reads the default region from driftscope/config.py:
"sundarbans": Region(
    "Sundarbans Delta", 88.0, 90.5, 21.0, 22.8,
    seed_lon=89.0, seed_lat=21.2,
),
…and downloads CMEMS surface currents (variables uo, vo) for that bbox over the trailing 14 days, using the copernicusmarine Python client. Output:
data/currents/sundarbans_delta_<start>_<end>.nc
The file holds two velocity components on a (time, latitude, longitude) grid at 1/12° (≈ 8 km) resolution, daily means.






Tip



Caching by filename. output_path() builds a deterministic name from (region, start, end). If you re-run the command, it sees the file already exists and skips the download. To force a refetch, pass --force.




4.2.2 Step 2 — run a simulation
python -m driftscope.simulate calls driftscope/simulate.py:165’s run_simulation(). With no arguments it picks the most recently fetched currents file, seeds 500 particles in a small disk around the region’s default release point, and integrates for 10 days using fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) on the velocity field.
The output is a Zarr archive:
data/trajectories/sundarbans_delta_<start>_<end>__currents_only_traj.zarr/
Each particle is one row; each saved time step is one column. By default positions are saved every 3 hours over 10 days → 81 time steps.


4.2.3 Step 3 — quick plot
The one-liner uses load_trajectories() and traj_to_dataframe() from driftscope/viz.py to flatten the Zarr into a long-format pandas DataFrame, then a scatter on (lon, lat) colored by time.
The result is the simplest legitimate visualization of a Lagrangian simulation: every dot is one particle at one moment.


4.2.4 Step 4 — dashboard
app.py is a Streamlit app. The sidebar lets you change region, runtime, seed point, and forcings without touching the CLI; three tabs show drift trails, accumulation heatmap, and the underlying velocity field.
It’s a useful exploration tool but not where the work happens. The authoritative interface is the Python API.

4.3 What you can do next
Three productive directions, each one chapter of this book:

Understand the physics — why does the trajectory bend the way it does? Start with Chapter 5.
Add a forcing — currents alone miss tides, waves, and wind. Add them with the patterns in Chapter 8 and see how the trajectory changes.
Validate against reality — overlay a real Global Drifter Program track on a simulated one and compute a skill score. Chapter 19.

4.4 Common quickstart issues






Note





copernicusmarine asks for credentials interactively. It means COPERNICUSMARINE_USERNAME and COPERNICUSMARINE_PASSWORD aren’t in your environment. Make sure you actually edited .env, and that load_dotenv() is finding it (run from the repo root).

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
text:
5 The Lagrangian frame
Two ways to describe a moving fluid. Both correct, both useful, but only one answers the question “where will this particle end up?”

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
text:
5.1 Eulerian vs Lagrangian
Stand on a bridge over a river. Two ways to take measurements:

Eulerian. Fix a station under the bridge. At every moment, record the velocity at that location. You get \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}, t)\) — a field. Repeat at many stations and you have a velocity map. CMEMS and HYCOM are Eulerian products: a velocity at every grid cell.
Lagrangian. Drop a leaf in. Walk along the bank with it. Record its position at every moment. You get \(\mathbf{X}(t)\) — a trajectory.

The two frames are linked by a single ODE:
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{X}(t)}{dt} \;=\; \mathbf{u}\!\left(\mathbf{X}(t),\, t\right)
\tag{5.1}\]
The leaf’s velocity at any moment is whatever the velocity field is at the leaf’s location at that moment. Read this carefully: the right-hand side is evaluated at \(\mathbf{X}(t)\), not at any fixed point. As the leaf moves through the field, it experiences different velocities. The trajectory is the integral of this co-moving velocity from the release point.






Tip



Why “Lagrangian”? After Joseph-Louis Lagrange, who in the 1780s framed mechanics in terms of trajectories of individual bodies. “Eulerian” honors Euler, who developed the field-based formulation a few decades earlier. The dichotomy is older than oceanography, and you’ll meet it in atmospheric science, plasma physics, and even computer graphics (particle systems).

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
section: 5.2 Why the leaf doesn’t trace a streamline
text:
5.2 Why the leaf doesn’t trace a streamline
A common confusion: aren’t trajectories the same as the streamlines you see on a current map?
No. Streamlines are tangent to the velocity field at a fixed instant. They are integrals of the field at one frozen moment. A trajectory is an integral through time. If the field is steady (doesn’t change with time), they coincide. Real ocean fields change continuously: tides every 12 h, synoptic features every few days, the eddy field every 1–4 weeks. Over a 10-day simulation, the leaf samples many different streamline patterns.
We only get a trajectory if we integrate Eq. 5.1 through a time-varying field. That is what driftscope/simulate.py does, ~500 lines of plumbing on top of OceanParcels’ RK4 integrator.

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
text:
5.3 The DriftScope master equation
Real surface objects don’t drift purely with the resolved Eulerian current. Several other terms move them. We collect all of them into one master equation:
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt}
= \mathbf{u}_\text{currents}
+ \mathbf{u}_\text{Stokes}
+ \mathbf{u}_\text{tides}
+ \alpha\,\mathbf{u}_{10}
+ \mathbf{w}_\text{settle}
+ \boldsymbol{\eta}_t
\tag{5.2}\]
term by term:









Symbol
What it represents
Where it comes from
Chapter




\(\mathbf{u}_\text{currents}\)
Eulerian surface current — the dominant term over open water
CMEMS GLORYS analysis or HYCOM ESPC
Chapter 11


\(\mathbf{u}_\text{Stokes}\)
Wave-induced drift; second-order in wave amplitude
Derived from ERA5 wave height and period
Chapter 8


\(\mathbf{u}_\text{tides}\)
Barotropic tidal currents; the dominant signal in shallow shelves
Predicted from TPXO9 harmonics via pyTMD
Chapter 8


\(\alpha\,\mathbf{u}_{10}\)
Direct wind drag on emergent fraction of the object (“windage”)
ERA5 10 m winds × empirical coefficient \(\alpha\)
Chapter 8


\(\mathbf{w}_\text{settle}\)
Vertical settling velocity for a sinking particle (SPM)
Stokes’ law; depends on grain size
Chapter 9


\(\boldsymbol{\eta}_t\)
Stochastic random walk parameterizing unresolved sub-grid eddies
White-noise process with diffusivity \(K_h\)
Chapter 10



Each term is an independent module. The architectural payoff: to add a new physics — say, biological vertical migration — you write one velocity field or one kernel, and bolt it onto the right-hand side.

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
section: 5.4 What the right-hand side is not
text:
5.4 What the right-hand side is not
A few legitimate ocean processes are missing from Eq. 5.2 and worth naming:

Inertia. Real particles have mass; Eq. 5.2 assumes they follow the flow exactly. For micron-scale sediment, mass is negligible and this is an excellent approximation. For macro-debris (lost shipping containers, floating rafts of trees) it isn’t, and you’d need a Maxey–Riley equation.
Buoyancy and surface trapping. A ping-pong ball rises faster than the surrounding water can take it down. We ignore vertical exchange except for the explicit settling term.
Surface tension and Langmuir circulation. Both can sort floating material into windrows on horizontal scales of meters to hundreds of meters. CMEMS doesn’t see them. The Brownian random walk crudely lumps this into “unresolved variability.”







Warning



Lying to yourself with smooth fields. A common Lagrangian-modeling sin is treating Eq. 5.2 as if all terms were known exactly. They are not. CMEMS at 1/12° smooths over the entire submesoscale field; tidal models have 5–10% error in shelf seas; ERA5 winds are coarsely sampled. The trajectory is a consequence of all those errors compounding. Always quote your forcings and their resolution — the validation chapter makes this concrete.

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
text:
5.5 A concrete picture
Here’s the data path for one DriftScope particle, in plain English:

The particle is released at \((\text{lon}_0, \text{lat}_0, t_0)\).
At each time step (default 30 minutes), simulate.py interpolates each forcing field at the particle’s current position to get a velocity vector.
The velocities are summed.
The integrator (RK4) advances the position by 30 minutes’ worth of that velocity, with three additional probes within the step to get higher-order accuracy.
The new position is recorded if the output cadence (default 3 h) ticks over.
Repeat until \(t_0 + \text{runtime}\).

That’s the whole simulation. Everything else in this book is “what’s in step 2 for term X?” or “how do we make sure step 4 doesn’t drift?”

title: 4  The Lagrangian frame
text:
5.6 Reading the code
driftscope/simulate.py:165 — the run_simulation() function — is where Eq. 5.2 meets Python. Skim it now if you can:

Lines 201–222: which forcings are active? Build a single combined velocity NetCDF with combine_forcings().
Lines 248–267: hand the combined field to OceanParcels as a FieldSet.
Lines 269–331: build the seed cloud (where particles start).
Lines 380–397: the kernel chain, which is [AdvectionRK4, Settling?, BrownianMotion2D?, DeleteOOB] depending on flags.
Line 392: pset.execute(...) — the actual run.

Don’t worry about understanding every line yet. The next five chapters make every line make sense.

title: 5  Advection and RK4
text:
6 Advection and RK4
The integrator is the engine. This chapter explains why DriftScope uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta, what its alternatives would look like, and how OceanParcels actually does the work.

title: 5  Advection and RK4
text:
6.1 The problem
We need to solve
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt} = \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{X}, t)
\]
starting from \(\mathbf{X}(t_0) = \mathbf{X}_0\). The right-hand side is known only at discrete grid points and discrete time steps — we have a NetCDF, not an analytic function. So:

We need a way to evaluate \(\mathbf{u}\) at arbitrary \((\mathbf{x}, t)\) in space–time. That is interpolation.
We need a way to step \(\mathbf{X}\) forward in time using \(\mathbf{u}\). That is time integration.

These two pieces are mostly orthogonal. Bad interpolation can ruin a good integrator (and vice versa). DriftScope uses bilinear-in-space + linear-in-time interpolation, and RK4 in time. Let’s see why each.

title: 5  Advection and RK4
text:
6.2 Why not just Euler?
The simplest integrator is forward Euler:
\[
\mathbf{X}_{n+1} = \mathbf{X}_n + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{X}_n, t_n)
\tag{6.1}\]
Evaluate the velocity at where you are now, push the particle that direction for \(\Delta t\). One velocity probe per step, dead simple.
It is also wrong, in a specific way. Euler has first-order local truncation error: per step, you accumulate error \(\propto \Delta t^2\), and over a fixed total time the global error is \(\propto \Delta t\). Halve the time step, halve the error. This converges, but slowly. For a 10-day simulation in a shear-rich field, you’d need \(\Delta t < 5\) minutes to get a usable answer. That’s \(\sim 3000\) velocity probes per particle.
Worse, Euler is unstable in any rotational flow: a particle in a circular eddy spirals outward instead of orbiting. After one synthetic eddy period, the trajectory is unrecognizable. Bad.

title: 5  Advection and RK4
text:
6.3 RK4: four probes, fourth-order accuracy
Runge–Kutta 4 is the workhorse compromise between accuracy and computational cost. The recipe:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{X}_n, t_n) \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= \mathbf{u}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf{k}_1,\; t_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\right) \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= \mathbf{u}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf{k}_2,\; t_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\right) \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= \mathbf{u}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf{k}_3,\; t_n + \Delta t\right) \\
\mathbf{X}_{n+1} &= \mathbf{X}_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{6}(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4)
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.2}\]
In words: probe the velocity at the start of the step (\(\mathbf{k}_1\)), then at the midpoint using \(\mathbf{k}_1\) as the slope (\(\mathbf{k}_2\)), then again at the midpoint using the better \(\mathbf{k}_2\) as the slope (\(\mathbf{k}_3\)), then at the endpoint using \(\mathbf{k}_3\) (\(\mathbf{k}_4\)). Take a weighted average — endpoints get weight 1, midpoints get weight 2 — and that is the slope for the step.
Costs four velocity probes per step. Pays back as \(O(\Delta t^4)\) local error and \(O(\Delta t^4)\) global error over fixed time. Halving \(\Delta t\) cuts error by \(16\times\). RK4 with \(\Delta t = 30\) min beats Euler with \(\Delta t = 1\) min in both accuracy and cost.
In a steady linear shear, RK4 also conserves energy to machine precision — no spurious spiraling.






Tip



The “Magic of RK4” sounds suspicious. Where does the fourth-order accuracy come from? Each midpoint probe captures one more term of the Taylor expansion of \(\mathbf{u}(t)\), and the weighted average is hand-tuned to cancel error terms up to fourth order. RK4 is the minimum-cost explicit scheme that achieves order 4 — there is no order-4 scheme with three or fewer evaluations. RK5 needs six. RK6 needs seven. Past four, the cost grows faster than the accuracy gain for typical ocean problems, which is why RK4 has been the default in every Lagrangian framework since the 1980s.

title: 5  Advection and RK4
text:
6.4 The Parcels implementation
OceanParcels (the framework DriftScope uses) ships a JIT-compiled AdvectionRK4 kernel. We use it directly:
from parcels import AdvectionRK4   # in driftscope/simulate.py:191
The kernel is just Eq. 6.2 written in a small DSL that Parcels JITs to C. For reference, the equivalent custom kernel — which we use when we want to gracefully delete particles that hit land — lives in driftscope/kernels.py:50:
def AdvectionRK4_Land(particle, fieldset, time):
    (u1, v1) = fieldset.UV[particle]
    lon1 = particle.lon + u1 * 0.5 * particle.dt
    lat1 = particle.lat + v1 * 0.5 * particle.dt

    (u2, v2) = fieldset.UV[time + 0.5 * particle.dt, particle.depth, lat1, lon1, particle]
    lon2 = particle.lon + u2 * 0.5 * particle.dt
    lat2 = particle.lat + v2 * 0.5 * particle.dt

    (u3, v3) = fieldset.UV[time + 0.5 * particle.dt, particle.depth, lat2, lon2, particle]
    lon3 = particle.lon + u3 * particle.dt
    lat3 = particle.lat + v3 * particle.dt

    (u4, v4) = fieldset.UV[time + particle.dt, particle.depth, lat3, lon3, particle]

    particle_dlon += (u1 + 2 * u2 + 2 * u3 + u4) / 6.0 * particle.dt
    particle_dlat += (v1 + 2 * v2 + 2 * v3 + v4) / 6.0 * particle.dt
Read line by line — it is exactly Eq. 6.2 in code. The four UV[...] reads are the four velocity probes. The final two lines accumulate the position update; Parcels then writes them to particle.lon, particle.lat after the kernel chain finishes.






Note



particle_dlon and particle_dlat are magic identifiers that Parcels recognizes. You don’t declare them; the JIT compiler resolves them to private accumulators per particle. Ditto particle_ddepth for the vertical component (used in Chapter 9). The noqa: F821 annotations in the source silence linters that don’t know about this.

title: 5  Advection and RK4
text:
6.5 Choosing \(\Delta t\)
DriftScope’s default integration step is 30 minutes (SimConfig.dt_minutes = 30, in driftscope/config.py). This is small enough that RK4 stays well below 1 km position error per day in typical Bay of Bengal flows (peak speed ~1 m/s). Smaller is wasteful; larger and you start to see the trajectory cross multiple grid cells per step, which the linear interpolation can’t represent honestly.
Two regimes flip that default:

Tides on. When you add tidal forcing the field has hourly variability with peak speeds of 1–2 m/s in the Sundarbans. The combined field is re-gridded onto a 1-hour time axis (see driftscope/simulate.py:91), and the 30-minute step is then short enough that you see the M2 oscillation.
Output cadence. Distinct from the integration step: you don’t have to save every step. Default is output_minutes = 180 (every 3 h), which gives 81 saved positions over 10 days — plenty for plotting, animations, and statistics. The integration is the cost; saving is essentially free.







Tip



The CFL number, casually. A rule of thumb for stability: \(u_\text{max}
\Delta t / \Delta x < 1\). With \(u_\text{max} \approx 1\) m/s and CMEMS \(\Delta x \approx 8000\) m, \(\Delta t < 8000\) s (\(\approx 2\) h) keeps you safe. Our 30-minute step has plenty of headroom; doubling to 1 hour would still be stable for currents-only runs. In tidal regimes the grid is unchanged but \(u_\text{max}\) doubles — still safe at 30 min.

5  Advection and RK4
text:
6.7 Summary

DriftScope integrates Eq. 5.2 with RK4 at 30-minute steps.
Trajectories are bilinearly interpolated in space, linearly in time. Both are configurable but rarely worth changing.
Particles are JIT-compiled to C — runtime is dominated by NetCDF I/O, not the integrator.
DeleteOOB turns out-of-bounds errors into clean particle deletion, making coastal simulations practical.

The next chapter moves from the integrator to the first non-trivial physical phenomenon you encounter on a rotating planet: the Coriolis force, and the inertial period that pops out of Eq. 6.2 when you run it through a uniform field.

title: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period
text:
7 Coriolis and the inertial period
We’re on a rotating planet. Anything moving freely in a horizontal plane feels a sideways pseudo-force. This chapter explains the Coriolis parameter \(f\), the inertial period \(T_i = 2\pi / f\), and where they show up in the DriftScope diagnostics.
crumbs: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period

title: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period
section: 7.1 Why a sideways force shows up
text:
7.1 Why a sideways force shows up
In a non-rotating frame, Newton’s second law is \(\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}\). In a frame rotating at angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\), the equation gains two pseudo-forces:
\[
m\,\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{dt}
= \mathbf{F} - 2m\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{u}
- m\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{r})
\tag{7.1}\]
The first new term is the Coriolis force, the second is centrifugal. For ocean dynamics on Earth, centrifugal is absorbed into apparent gravity (it just shifts what we call “down”). What remains, projected onto a horizontal plane at latitude \(\varphi\), is
\[
\frac{du}{dt} = +f\,v, \qquad \frac{dv}{dt} = -f\,u
\tag{7.2}\]
with the Coriolis parameter
\[
f \;=\; 2\Omega \sin\varphi \;\approx\; 1.458\times 10^{-4}\,\sin\varphi \quad [\text{s}^{-1}]
\tag{7.3}\]
where \(\Omega = 7.2921\times 10^{-5}\) rad/s is Earth’s angular velocity. Sign matters: \(f\) is positive in the Northern Hemisphere, negative in the Southern, zero on the equator.






Tip



Where does the factor of 2 come from? It’s the Coriolis \(-2\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{u}\) projected onto the horizontal — only the vertical component of \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) (\(= \Omega \sin\varphi\)) acts on horizontal motion. The factor 2 falls out of the cross-product algebra. See Phillips (1977) §1.5 for the derivation.
crumbs: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period

title: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period
text:
7.2 The inertial oscillation
Suppose nothing else acts on a parcel of water — no pressure gradient, no friction, no wind. Just Coriolis. Then Eq. 7.2 is a coupled linear ODE with eigenvalues \(\pm if\). The solution is
\[
u(t) = U_0 \cos(ft) + V_0 \sin(ft), \qquad
v(t) = -U_0 \sin(ft) + V_0 \cos(ft)
\]
A circle of radius \(|U|/f\), traced clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere (anticlockwise in the South), with period
\[
T_i \;=\; \frac{2\pi}{|f|}
\tag{7.4}\]
Plug in the Sundarbans latitude \(\varphi = 22°\text{N}\):
\[
f \approx 5.46\times 10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}, \qquad T_i \approx 32.0 \text{ h}
\]
A patch of water given a kick will trace a roughly 32-hour circle and return near where it started. Real ocean trajectories, of course, don’t do this cleanly — there’s always a pressure gradient, friction, etc. — but the inertial period is a fundamental timescale of the system.






Note



The Bay of Bengal has a particularly clear inertial signal: it sits in the trade-wind belt, gets episodic monsoon “kicks”, and has weak background flow over much of its central basin. Drifter spectra often show a clean peak at \(T_i \approx 32\) h. CMEMS daily means hide this peak (daily averaging is a low-pass filter that kills 32-h signals) — which is why DriftScope’s currents-only validation against drifters tends to underestimate short-time scatter.
crumbs: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period

title: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period
text:
7.3 \(f\) in the codebase
The Coriolis parameter shows up explicitly only in the diagnostics module — the integrator doesn’t need it because it’s already implicit in any Eulerian velocity field that obeys the equations of motion. From driftscope/diagnostics.py:18:
OMEGA = 7.2921e-5        # rad/s
...
f = 2 * OMEGA * np.sin(np.deg2rad(LAT2D))
It’s used in two normalized diagnostics:
\[
\frac{\zeta}{f} = \frac{\partial v / \partial x - \partial u / \partial y}{f},
\qquad
\frac{\delta}{f} = \frac{\partial u / \partial x + \partial v / \partial y}{f}
\tag{7.5}\]
The first is relative vorticity (rotation of the flow at a point) over \(f\). The second is divergence over \(f\). Both are dimensionless. Both are flavors of Rossby number — measures of how strongly the flow deviates from geostrophic balance.







\(\zeta / f\)
What it means




\(\ll 1\)
Geostrophic flow; rotation negligible compared to background spin


\(\sim 0.5\)
Strong eddies, frontal regions


\(\gtrsim 1\)
Submesoscale dynamics; cyclostrophic balance


Very high
The model is probably resolving features it shouldn’t



A real submesoscale-resolving product (GOFLOW, the figure that started this book) shows \(\zeta / f\) filaments stronger than \(\pm 1\). CMEMS at 1/12° and HYCOM at 1/25° barely reach \(\pm 0.5\), even at the strongest eddy edges — they smooth over the dynamics that produce \(|\zeta/f| > 1\).

title: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period
text:
7.5 \(\beta\) and what we’re ignoring
Strictly, \(f\) varies with latitude: \(f = f_0 + \beta y\) where \(\beta = df/dy\). This \(\beta\)-effect drives Rossby waves and the western intensification of boundary currents. Over the few-degrees latitude range of a typical DriftScope run, \(\beta y \ll f_0\) and the constant-\(f\) approximation is fine for a single trajectory. Over basin-scale runs (full Bay of Bengal, months) it matters; CMEMS already includes it implicitly because the model that produced CMEMS solves the full equations.
A reader who wants to push this further should read Phillips (1977) chapters 3–4 for the wave dynamics, then Geyer & MacCready (2014) for the estuarine context.

title: 6  Coriolis and the inertial period
text:
7.6 Summary

Coriolis is a frame-of-reference effect; on a rotating planet, horizontal motion couples through Eq. 7.2.
The inertial period \(T_i = 2\pi/f\) is a fundamental ocean timescale; \(\approx 32\) h at Sundarbans, \(\approx 17\) h at 45° latitude.
\(f\) shows up in DriftScope only in diagnostics, where \(\zeta/f\) and \(\delta/f\) measure how strongly the flow deviates from geostrophic balance.
Daily-mean currents (CMEMS, HYCOM) filter out inertial oscillations. The drifter-validation chapter shows what gets lost.

title: 7  Stokes drift, tides, and windage
text:
8 Stokes drift, tides, and windage
CMEMS gives you “currents” but not all of them. Three additional velocity contributions matter for surface objects, especially in shallow shelves and during energetic weather:
DriftScope adds all three at the data layer: each has its own NetCDF, each is interpolated to the currents grid, all are summed before the integrator runs. driftscope/simulate.py:47’s combine_forcings() is where this happens. The architectural reason to do it at data-layer (not in a kernel) is that interpolation and summation are cheap, parallelizable, and don’t need to run inside the JIT-compiled integration loop.
crumbs: 7  Stokes drift, tides, and windage

title: 7  Stokes drift, tides, and windage
text:
8.1 Stokes drift
A pure linear wave looks like a sinusoidal up-and-down at every point — nothing should drift. But surface waves are not exactly linear. To second order in wave amplitude, a fluid parcel under the waves experiences a small mean displacement in the direction the waves are going. This is Stokes drift, derived by Stokes (1847).
For a single sinusoid of amplitude \(a\), period \(T\), wavenumber \(k = 2\pi/L\):
\[
U_s(z) \;=\; \omega k a^2\, e^{2 k z}
\;=\; \frac{(2\pi)^2}{T^2} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{L} \cdot a^2 \cdot e^{2 k z}
\tag{8.1}\]
with \(z = 0\) at the surface and \(z < 0\) below. The drift falls off exponentially below the surface; for a 10-second swell (\(L \approx 156\) m), the e-folding scale is about 12 m.
For a broadband wave field, the surface (\(z = 0\)) Stokes drift is
\[
U_s \;\approx\; \frac{(2\pi)^3 H_s^2}{8\,g\,T_m^3}
\tag{8.2}\]
where \(H_s\) is the significant wave height and \(T_m\) is the mean wave period. This is the deep-water surface formula DriftScope uses; see driftscope/stokes.py:56:
def stokes_from_waves(swh, mwp, mwd):
    magnitude = (2 * np.pi) ** 3 * swh ** 2 / (8 * G * mwp ** 3)
    theta = np.deg2rad(270.0 - mwd)
    ust = magnitude * np.cos(theta)
    vst = magnitude * np.sin(theta)
    ...






Tip



The angle conversion is a classic gotcha. ERA5’s mwd is the meteorological convention: the direction the waves come from, in degrees clockwise from North. We need the math angle: where they’re going, in radians counterclockwise from East. The transformation is math_angle = 270° − mwd. If you forget the sign, your particles drift the wrong way for a few weeks before someone notices.



8.1.1 Magnitudes in the Bay of Bengal
Plug in monsoon-season values: \(H_s \approx 2.5\) m, \(T_m \approx 8\) s.
\[
U_s \approx \frac{(2\pi)^3 \cdot 6.25}{8 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 512} \approx 0.038 \text{ m/s}
\]
So \(\sim 4\) cm/s during peak monsoon — small compared to the 0.2–0.5 m/s typical CMEMS surface currents, but not negligible over a 10-day simulation. Pre-monsoon and post-monsoon values are 1–2 cm/s.


8.1.2 Why a coefficient
The factor \((2\pi)^3 / (8g)\) in Eq. 8.2 assumes a narrow-band spectrum. Real wave spectra have spread, and different conventions assign different prefactors. OpenDrift uses \(\sim 8\pi^3 / g\), which is roughly \(8\times\) larger than ours. DriftScope exposes a stokes_scale knob in SimConfig so a student can experiment with this prefactor. We default to 1.0 (narrow-band textbook formula) and document this choice in the validation chapter.
crumbs: 7  Stokes drift, tides, and windage

title: 7  Stokes drift, tides, and windage
text:
8.2 Tides
Tidal currents are deterministic. Given a location and a moment in time, a calibrated harmonic model (TPXO9, FES2014, OTIS) tells you the barotropic \((u_\text{tide}, v_\text{tide})\) exactly. CMEMS GLORYS filters tides out during data assimilation — it would otherwise need to be assimilating 6-hourly tide-gauge data, which it doesn’t. So if you want tides, you have to add them.
In the Sundarbans, tides dominate everything else. Spring tides reach 1–1.5 m/s. CMEMS surface currents in the same place are 0.2–0.4 m/s (monsoon residual), 0.05–0.1 m/s (dry season). A particle simulation without tides in a delta region is physically wrong.

8.2.1 Harmonic prediction in 200 words
A tide model is a sum of sinusoids:
\[
u_\text{tide}(\mathbf{x}, t) = \sum_n A_n(\mathbf{x}) \cos\!\left[\omega_n t - \phi_n(\mathbf{x})\right]
\]
where \(\omega_n\) and \(\phi_n\) are the frequency and phase of constituent \(n\). The big ones are \(M_2\) (12.42 h, principal lunar semidiurnal), \(S_2\) (12.00 h, principal solar semidiurnal), \(K_1\) (23.93 h, lunisolar diurnal), and \(O_1\) (25.82 h, principal lunar diurnal). TPXO9-atlas-v5 has 13 constituents on a 1/30° global grid.
The amplitude \(A_n(\mathbf{x})\) and phase \(\phi_n(\mathbf{x})\) are fitted once, by inverse modeling against tide gauges and altimetry Egbert & Erofeeva (2002). Prediction is then trivial: evaluate the sum.
DriftScope wraps this with pyTMD — see driftscope/tides.py:121:
res = pyTMD.compute.tide_currents(
    xx, yy, tt, component="u",
    directory=str(model_dir),
    model="TPXO9-atlas-v5-nc",
    epoch=(2000, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0),
    type="drift",
    standard="UTC",
    crs=4326,
    method="linear",
    extrapolate=False,
    crop=True,
    bounds=bounds, buffer=1.0,
)
The output is hourly \(u_\text{tide}\) and \(v_\text{tide}\) on the currents grid — see Chapter 13 for the data-side details and the seven pyTMD 3.x quirks the project navigated.






Tip



Tide-aware time grid. When you turn on tides, the simulation’s combined forcing NetCDF gets re-gridded onto the tides’ hourly time axis (see simulate.py:91). The currents (daily) are forward-filled to each hour. This preserves the full \(M_2\) oscillation that would otherwise be averaged away if we kept the daily grid.

title: 7  Stokes drift, tides, and windage
text:
8.3 Windage
Floating objects with parts above the waterline get pushed by the wind in addition to the water. The standard parameterization is empirical:
\[
\mathbf{u}_\text{windage} = \alpha\,\mathbf{u}_{10}
\tag{8.3}\]
where \(\mathbf{u}_{10}\) is the 10 m wind and \(\alpha\) is a small empirical windage coefficient that depends on the air-to-water profile of the object:



\(\alpha\)
Object class




0.01
Icebergs (mostly underwater)


0.02
Persons in water; sediment-laden water


0.02–0.04
Plastic debris (depends on shape)


0.03
DriftScope default; reasonable for general “buoyant material”


0.035
Oil slicks



The number is small but the wind is fast. Monsoon winds in the Bay of Bengal hit 10 m/s easily, so \(\alpha \mathbf{u}_{10}\) is 0.2–0.4 m/s — a big chunk of the surface velocity, comparable to or exceeding \(\mathbf{u}_\text{currents}\).






Warning



Don’t double-count Ekman. CMEMS already represents wind-driven Ekman currents in its surface flow (the model assimilates wind forcing). Windage is the additional direct drag on the emergent fraction of the object, on top of CMEMS + Stokes + tides. Don’t add it for a fully submerged particle (e.g. SPM at 1 m depth).


In code, windage is one numpy multiplication during the data-layer combine step (simulate.py:129):
u10 = wnd["u10"].interp({...}, time=time_grid).fillna(0.0) * windage_coeff
v10 = wnd["v10"].interp({...}, time=time_grid).fillna(0.0) * windage_coeff
uo = uo + u10
vo = vo + v10
That’s it. There’s no kernel for windage — once you’ve combined the velocity fields, the integrator doesn’t need to know which term came from which physics.

8.4 Putting them together
When you run a coupled simulation:
python -m driftscope.simulate \
    --stokes data/waves/<file>.nc \
    --tides data/tides/<file>.nc \
    --winds data/winds/<file>.nc \
    --windage 0.02

The cache filename encodes which forcings are active:
sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01__stokes1.0_tides_wind2.0pct.nc
so different combos don’t collide and reruns are idempotent.

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
text:
9 Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
A real sediment grain isn’t a tracer that follows the flow — it falls through it. Slowly. The vertical fall speed sets where it ends up relative to a perfect-tracer particle. This chapter derives the settling velocity, sites it in the DriftScope kernel chain, and explains the range of validity.
crumbs: 8  Settling — Stokes' law for SPM

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
text:
9.1 Stokes’ law
A small spherical particle of density \(\rho_p\) and diameter \(d\) falling through a fluid of density \(\rho_w\) and viscosity \(\mu\) has terminal velocity (downward positive):
\[
w_s \;=\; \frac{(\rho_p - \rho_w)\,g\,d^2}{18\,\mu}
\;=\; \frac{2}{9}\,\frac{(\rho_p - \rho_w)\,g\,r^2}{\mu}
\tag{9.1}\]
with \(r = d/2\). Derived by Stokes (1851) by balancing buoyancy (\(-\rho_w g V\)), gravity (\(\rho_p g V\)), and the viscous drag on a sphere at low Reynolds number (\(6\pi \mu r u\)). Set the net force to zero and solve for \(u\) — that’s \(w_s\).
The DriftScope helper function lives at driftscope/kernels.py:27:
def stokes_settling_velocity(diameter_um, particle_density_kg_m3=2650.0,
                             water_density_kg_m3=1025.0,
                             viscosity_pa_s=1.002e-3):
    r = (diameter_um * 1e-6) / 2.0
    return ((2.0 / 9.0) *
            (particle_density_kg_m3 - water_density_kg_m3) /
            viscosity_pa_s * GRAVITY * r * r)






Tip



Why \(r^2\)? The drag force scales linearly with size (\(6\pi\mu r u\)), but the gravitational drive scales with volume (\(\rho V \propto r^3\)). Volume divided by drag gives \(r^2\). Larger particles fall much faster. A \(50\,\mu\)m grain falls \(25\times\) faster than a \(10\,\mu\)m grain.

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
text:
9.3 When Stokes’ law breaks
Eq. 9.1 assumes:

Stokes flow around the sphere — particle Reynolds number \(Re_p =
d\,w_s\,\rho_w/\mu < 0.5\).
Spherical particles.
Single particle in dilute suspension (no neighbors).
Newtonian fluid at constant viscosity.

For SPM in seawater: assumption 1 holds up to \(d \approx 80\) µm. Beyond that, the wake separates and Stokes’ law overpredicts \(w_s\).
For real estuarine sediment: assumption 2 fails badly. Clay particles are plates, silt grains are angular, and flocculation glues them into porous flocs that can be 10–100 µm aggregates of 1 µm primary particles. A floc settles slower than a single \(10\,\mu\)m grain because its effective density (water-saturated mineral) is much lower than \(\rho_p\). Real-world \(w_s\) for “10 µm silt” in a turbid estuary is often 1–3 m/day, not 8.






Warning



The settling-velocity calibration is the single largest uncertainty in SPM transport modeling, and it varies by season, salinity, and SPM concentration itself. DriftScope’s default is “single mineral grain at mid-shelf salinity” — fine for a teaching tutorial; not fine for a calibrated regulatory model.


DriftScope makes the assumption explicit by exposing settling_diameter_um and settling_density_kg_m3 in SimConfig:
@dataclass
class SimConfig:
    ...
    include_settling: bool = False
    settling_diameter_um: float = 10.0
    settling_density_kg_m3: float = 2650.0

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
section: 9.4 Why settling is a kernel, not a field
text:
9.4 Why settling is a kernel, not a field
Stokes drift, tides, and windage are added at the data layer — they’re spatial fields you sum into one combined NetCDF. Settling is different: it is a per-particle velocity that depends on the particle’s own properties (size, density). Two particles at the same location can have different settling velocities. So it has to live in a kernel — JIT-compiled code that runs per-particle inside the integration loop.
driftscope/kernels.py:86:
def Settling(particle, fieldset, time):
    """Stokes settling for SPM. Requires per-particle `w_settle` (m/s, +down)."""
    particle_ddepth += particle.w_settle * particle.dt
Three lines, one of them a comment. The accumulator particle_ddepth is Parcels’ magic identifier for “increment the depth by this much” — same pattern as particle_dlon, particle_dlat from Chapter 6.
The per-particle attribute w_settle is set up in simulate.py:235 when settling is enabled:
class SedimentParticle(JITParticle):
    w_settle = Variable("w_settle", dtype=np.float32, initial=w_s)
ParticleClass = SedimentParticle
Every particle gets the same w_s initially, but you could subclass SedimentParticle to give each particle a different size — trivially extending the framework to handle a poly-disperse SPM population. We don’t do that yet; one constant for now.
crumbs: 8  Settling — Stokes' law for SPM

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
text:
9.5 Kernel chain order
The kernel chain runs once per integration step, in order:
# simulate.py:385
kernels = [AdvectionRK4]
if use_settling: kernels.append(Settling)
if use_brownian: kernels.append(BrownianMotion2D)
kernels.append(DeleteOOB)
Order matters. AdvectionRK4 first computes the horizontal step using the combined Eulerian velocity. Then Settling adds the vertical step. Then BrownianMotion2D adds horizontal noise. Then DeleteOOB cleans up. If you swapped settling and Brownian, the answer is the same to within \(\Delta t^2\) (operator-splitting error), so order between physics kernels mostly doesn’t matter — but we keep advection first by convention because it’s the primary motion.
crumbs: 8  Settling — Stokes' law for SPM

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
section: 9.6 What settling does to the trajectory
text:
9.6 What settling does to the trajectory
A particle that settles eventually leaves the surface velocity field and starts experiencing whatever subsurface velocities the model resolves. For CMEMS/HYCOM, “subsurface” means the next vertical level (depth ~5 m or so depending on dataset).
In practice:

Day 0: particle at \(z = 0\), surface drift dominates.
Day 1: \(z \approx -8\) m (default 10-µm silt). Still in the surface mixed layer in monsoon BoB; little change in horizontal velocity.
Day 5: \(z \approx -38\) m. Below the seasonal thermocline in pre-monsoon; horizontal velocity is much weaker, ~0.05 m/s.
Day 10: \(z \approx -76\) m. Mid-shelf or deeper. Particle has effectively decoupled from surface variability.

This means settled particles cluster under their release point more than perfect tracers do. The accumulation pattern in a coupled SPM run shows this: a higher concentration directly below the river mouth and along the shelf, less spread offshore than a no-settling run.






Tip



Compare with and without settling. Run the same simulation twice with include_settling = True/False and overlay the final-position scatter. The difference is the SPM-specific signal — what makes sediment behave differently from a passive tracer. See the validation tutorial for the plotting code.
crumbs: 8  Settling — Stokes' law for SPM

title: 8  Settling — Stokes’ law for SPM
text:
9.7 Summary

Settling velocity is given by Stokes’ law for small spherical particles in laminar flow, Eq. 9.1.
For 10 µm silt-class quartz, \(w_s \approx 8\) m/day — meaningful over a 10-day simulation.
Real estuarine SPM forms flocs; effective \(w_s\) is reduced by 3–5×. DriftScope doesn’t model flocculation but exposes the settling parameters so a student can experiment.
Settling lives in a per-particle kernel rather than a velocity field, because it depends on particle properties (size, density).
The kernel chain runs AdvectionRK4 → Settling → BrownianMotion2D → DeleteOOB per step.

Next: the stochastic term — Brownian motion, the small random walk that parameterizes everything the model can’t resolve.




Stokes, G. G. (1851). On the effect of the internal friction of fluids on the motion of pendulums. Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 9, 8–106.
