title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10 Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
The Eulerian velocity field is smooth at the model grid scale. The real ocean is not. Eddies smaller than 1/12° (CMEMS) or 1/25° (HYCOM) are unresolved — they are real flow, but they don’t appear in the data. This chapter explains how DriftScope parameterizes these unresolved eddies as a stochastic random walk, and why that choice is conservative but honest.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.1 The unresolved-eddy problem
Run a noiseless DriftScope simulation against a real Global Drifter Program trajectory released at the same point. After a few days, the simulated and real drifters separate. The drifter’s trajectory has scale-rich wiggles on time scales of hours and length scales of 1–10 km. The simulated trajectory is smooth.
Why? Because the drifter is in a real eddy field. CMEMS at 1/12° smooths across submesoscale eddies (1–10 km) and chops the inertial-period band out of the daily mean. So a simulated trajectory misses two things:

Daily-mean filtering: inertial oscillations and sub-daily variance.
Spatial resolution: submesoscale eddies and fronts.

The combined effect is that the model is missing \(O(0.1\)–\(1)\) m/s of short-time, small-scale variability. Over 10 days at 0.3 m/s of unresolved drift, that’s a position error of ~250 km in any direction — roughly what DriftScope’s drifter-validation chapter shows for CMEMS-only runs.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.2 The simplest fix: random walk
A random walk added to the trajectory parameterizes the unresolved variability without claiming to model it explicitly. The mathematical object is a 2D Wiener process:
\[
d\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{u}\,dt + \sqrt{2 K_h}\,d\mathbf{W}
\tag{10.1}\]
where \(d\mathbf{W} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}\,dt)\) — two independent unit-variance Gaussian increments per step. \(K_h\) is the horizontal eddy diffusivity (m²/s) — the strength of the random forcing.
The discrete version DriftScope uses, per timestep:
\[
\Delta x = \sqrt{2 K_h |\Delta t|} \cdot \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad
\Delta y = \sqrt{2 K_h |\Delta t|} \cdot \mathcal{N}(0, 1)
\tag{10.2}\]
This adds a Gaussian-distributed kick to the particle’s position every step, with standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{2 K_h |\Delta t|}\).
driftscope/kernels.py:114:
def BrownianMotion2D(particle, fieldset, time):
    rx = ParcelsRandom.normalvariate(0.0, 1.0)
    ry = ParcelsRandom.normalvariate(0.0, 1.0)
    sigma = math.sqrt(2.0 * fieldset.Kh * math.fabs(particle.dt))
    dx_m = sigma * rx
    dy_m = sigma * ry
    deg_per_m_lon = 1.0 / (111320.0 * math.cos(particle.lat * math.pi / 180.0))
    particle_dlat += dy_m / 110574.0
    particle_dlon += dx_m * deg_per_m_lon






Tip



The unit conversion at the bottom. Brownian draws are in meters; the particle position is in degrees. The conversion uses 1° lat = 110,574 m and 1° lon = \(111,\!320 \cdot \cos(\varphi)\) m. JIT compilation can’t capture module-level Python constants, which is why the numbers are hardcoded inline — read driftscope/kernels.py:111 for the gotcha note.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.3 How big is \(K_h\)?
There is a literature on this; Phillips (1977) chapter 6 is the canonical discussion. Rough magnitudes:



\(K_h\) (m²/s)
Regime
Drift RMS spread per day




1
Coastal sheltered, weak eddies
0.4 km


10
Open shelf, low eddy energy
1.3 km


100
DriftScope default; open BoB
4.2 km


1000
Strong eddy field (Gulf Stream)
13 km


10000
Large-scale Atlantic gyres
42 km



The default \(K_h = 100\) m²/s is a Bay of Bengal-tuned number. It comes from the drifter validation: CMEMS-only runs miss an observed track by ~150 km at day 22, suggesting an unresolved-velocity scale of \(\sim 0.08\) m/s. Set \(K_h\) such that one day’s RMS spread is ~7 km (matches the observed scatter), which gives \(K_h \approx 280\) m²/s. We rounded to 100 to be conservative — undershooting the random walk leaves room for the deterministic model error, which we don’t want to hide behind random forcing.






Warning



Brownian is a parameterization, not physics. It says: “I don’t know what the unresolved velocities are, but on average they should add 4 km of RMS scatter per day.” It does not tell you about coherent submesoscale features (filaments, fronts), only about the mean energy of unresolved motion. The figure inspired by GOFLOW (Chapter 20) shows the real submesoscale field — adding \(K_h\) doesn’t recreate it; it just distributes the typical scatter.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.4 Diffusion vs dispersion
Two related concepts that students conflate:

Diffusion is the spread of an ensemble — many particles released at the same point. The cloud broadens as \(\sigma(t) = \sqrt{2 K_h t}\).
Dispersion is the spread induced by the mean shear — different particles at slightly different starting points end up far apart because they sample different velocities along the way. This happens without any random forcing.

In the Bay of Bengal, dispersion typically dominates diffusion at scales larger than 10 km. A 500-particle cloud released in a 10-km disk will spread to 100 km in 10 days mostly from shear, and the Brownian random walk adds only ~13 km on top.
This is why DriftScope’s dispersion plots (Chapter 18) look noisy even with \(K_h = 0\): the deterministic flow is doing most of the work.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.5 Reproducibility
Because Brownian draws are random, two runs with the same configuration give different answers. DriftScope passes a fixed seed to run_simulation() (default 42). The seed initializes both numpy’s RNG (used to place initial particles) and Parcels’ internal RNG (used inside JIT kernels). With the same seed, the run is bit-exact reproducible.
For ensemble work — running the same setup with many seeds to characterize the noise — pass different seeds and aggregate the results. The seasonal dispersion script does this; see Chapter 21.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.6 When to turn it off
For exploring the deterministic flow (which CMEMS or HYCOM features the model resolves, where eddies are, what the dominant trajectories look like) — turn Brownian off. Set include_brownian = False in SimConfig.
For operational drift forecasting (where will the spill go in 5 days, within what cone of uncertainty) — leave it on. The cone of uncertainty is what Brownian gives you.
A run with Brownian on but small \(K_h\) (\(1\) m²/s) is also a useful “smoothness check”: real CMEMS simulations are eddy-poor enough that you should be able to tell if your trajectory is plausibly noisy or is just plain wrong.

title: 9  Sub-grid diffusion — Brownian motion
text:
10.7 Summary

Resolved currents miss inertial-band and submesoscale variability.
DriftScope parameterizes this as a 2D Brownian random walk with diffusivity \(K_h\) (default 100 m²/s for the Bay of Bengal).
Implemented as a Parcels kernel after AdvectionRK4 — see driftscope/kernels.py:114.
It’s a statistical parameterization — it adds the right amount of scatter, not the right patterns. For the right patterns you need higher resolution data (Module 6 — GOFLOW).

This closes out the Physics part. We’ve walked through all six terms in Eq. 1:
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt} = \mathbf{u}_\text{currents} + \mathbf{u}_\text{Stokes} + \mathbf{u}_\text{tides} + \alpha\,\mathbf{u}_{10} + \mathbf{w}_\text{settle} + \boldsymbol{\eta}_t
\]
The next part walks through where each term comes from — the data sources, the resolution tradeoffs, and the on-disk schemas DriftScope uses to keep them aligned.




Phillips, O. M. (1977). The dynamics of the upper ocean. Cambridge University Press.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11 Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
The dominant velocity term in Eq. 1 comes from one of two analyses:
This chapter explains why we have two sources, what each delivers, and how they compare in the Bay of Bengal.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.1 CMEMS: the default
The Copernicus Marine Service’s Global Ocean Physics Analysis and Forecast (GLOBAL_ANALYSISFORECAST_PHY_001_024) is a daily-mean global ocean state estimate at 1/12° horizontal resolution and 50 vertical levels. It is what most operational and academic Lagrangian work uses for surface currents.
Behind the scenes:

Model: NEMO ocean model (1/12° ORCA grid).
Atmosphere: forced by ECMWF NWP fields (analysis/forecast).
Assimilation: SST (multi-sensor L4), altimetry (Jason, Sentinel-3, -6, AltiKa), in-situ T/S profiles (Argo, XBT, gliders).
Cadence: hourly hindcast available, daily means most common.

DriftScope uses the daily product. Hourly is available but each day is ~4× larger, and a 14-day BoB region is still ~10 MB at daily. We trade tidal/inertial detail (filtered out in daily averaging) for download speed and simplicity.
Variables we pull:

uo, vo — eastward / northward velocity (m/s) at the surface depth level (0.494 m).

The fetcher is one OPeNDAP-equivalent call via copernicusmarine.subset():
# driftscope/fetch.py:74
copernicusmarine.subset(
    dataset_id="cmems_mod_glo_phy-cur_anfc_0.083deg_P1D-m",
    variables=["uo", "vo"],
    minimum_longitude=88.0, maximum_longitude=90.5,
    minimum_latitude=21.0, maximum_latitude=22.8,
    start_datetime="2026-04-17T00:00:00",
    end_datetime="2026-05-01T00:00:00",
    minimum_depth=0.494, maximum_depth=0.494,
    output_filename="...",
)
Output schema:
Dimensions: (time, latitude, longitude)
Variables:
  uo: m/s, surface eastward
  vo: m/s, surface northward
Coordinates:
  time: datetime64[ns], daily 12:00 UTC
  latitude: float32, 1/12° spacing
  longitude: float32, 1/12° spacing






Tip



Why the awkward depth. CMEMS uses fixed depth levels and 0.494 m is the shallowest. It is not exactly the surface — it represents the 0–1 m vertical mean — but it’s close enough that we treat it as surface flow. For a properly surface-trapped tracer (the very top millimeter), you’d want a wave-resolving model, which CMEMS isn’t.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.2 HYCOM: the second opinion
The Naval Research Laboratory’s HYCOM ESPC-D-V02 (Earth System Prediction Capability, Data, Version 02) is a global HYCOM analysis at 1/25° native resolution, served as 0.04° lat × 0.08° lon. Twice as fine in latitude as CMEMS in the eastern Bay of Bengal.
We added it as a DriftScope source after a drifter-validation episode in April 2026: a real drifter (NOAA GDP ID 300534064293930) entered the BoB from the Andaman side and tracked southwest under what looked like a shelf eddy. The CMEMS-driven simulation missed this feature; the trajectory diverged northward by day 7. Skill score (Liu–Weisberg) on CMEMS: 0.701. Same simulation on HYCOM: 0.852. The eddy was resolved at 1/25° and missed at 1/12°.
The fetch is more involved than CMEMS because HYCOM’s THREDDS server serves daily files (one per variable per day), each ~3 GB globally. We use OPeNDAP byte-range subsetting to pull only the bbox at surface depth, getting ~30 KB per day per variable instead of 3 GB.
driftscope/hycom.py:99:
def fetch_hycom_currents(bbox, start_date, end_date, region_name, force):
    ...
    for day in days:
        u_url = _hycom_url(day, "u3z")     # one file per variable
        v_url = _hycom_url(day, "v3z")
        u = _open_hycom_subset(u_url, "water_u", bbox)
        v = _open_hycom_subset(v_url, "water_v", bbox)
        ...
The output schema is deliberately identical to CMEMS:
Variables: uo, vo
Coordinates: time, latitude, longitude
with the source noted in the file’s attrs["source"]. Anything downstream (simulate, viz, diagnostics) treats them interchangeably.






Warning



Coverage starts 2024-08-10. HYCOM ESPC-D-V02 is a new product. For historical work (pre-2024) you have to use CMEMS. For real-time and recent work, HYCOM is the better choice in the Bay of Bengal.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.3 A/B: why both?
Two equally-credible sources is a feature, not redundancy. Three reasons:

Validation: comparing the same simulation on both sources tells you what is robust (signals both models agree on) vs model-dependent (signals only one captures). The drifter chapter does this explicitly.
Resolution-limited diagnostics: the dynamics snapshot (Chapter 20) needs the highest-res velocity field available to resolve eddies. HYCOM wins.
Failover: when one source has an outage (HYCOM has weekly maintenance windows; CMEMS has occasional latency), the other usually works.

The drift validation script scripts/drifter_validation_compare.py runs the same simulation on both currents and overlays them on the real drifter for direct visual A/B. This is the most informative single image you can make of “model resolution matters”.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.4 File-naming convention
DriftScope uses filename suffixes to keep the two sources from colliding:
data/currents/
  sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01.nc          ← CMEMS (default, no suffix)
  sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01_hycom.nc    ← HYCOM
This is set in hycom.py:117:
out = CURRENTS_DIR / f"{region_name}_{start_date}_{end_date}_hycom.nc"
So you can fetch both for the same region/window without overwrites, and downstream scripts pick a specific one by name.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.5 Inside the NetCDF
Open one with xarray to see the schema:
import xarray as xr
ds = xr.open_dataset("data/currents/sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01_hycom.nc")
print(ds)
Yields something like:
<xarray.Dataset>
Dimensions:    (time: 15, latitude: 44, longitude: 32)
Coordinates:
  * time       (time) datetime64[ns] 2026-04-16T12:00:00 ... 2026-04-30T12:00:00
  * latitude   (latitude) float64 21.0 21.04 21.08 ... 22.64 22.68 22.72
  * longitude  (longitude) float64 88.0 88.08 88.16 ... 90.32 90.4 90.48
    depth      float64 0.0
Data variables:
    uo         (time, latitude, longitude) float32
    vo         (time, latitude, longitude) float32
Attributes:
    source:   HYCOM ESPC-D-V02 (Navy Operational, 1/25° lat × 1/12.5° lon)
A 14-day Sundarbans bbox is 15 time steps × 44 × 32 = 21,120 cells per variable, or about 170 KB total. CMEMS for the same bbox is roughly 15 × 30 × 31 = 14,000 cells — slightly smaller because the 1/12° grid is coarser. Both fit in memory comfortably for any region you’d realistically study.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.6 Land mask and missing data
CMEMS marks land cells as _FillValue (NaN after xarray decoding). HYCOM does the same. The simulator filters seed points that fall on NaN cells (simulate.py:294) and the DeleteOOB kernel removes any particle that wanders into NaN at run time.
For the Sundarbans the land mask is important — the Sundarbans bbox is ~50% land (mangrove forest). A region-fill (“bbox”) seeding mode oversamples uniformly across the bbox and keeps only ocean cells, giving a coastline-shaped release pattern. This is the right mode for “how does sediment from the whole shelf disperse” questions.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.7 How to fetch
The CLIs are uniform across both sources:
# CMEMS for a preset region, last 14 days
python -m driftscope.fetch

# CMEMS for a custom bbox / date range
python -m driftscope.fetch --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 --start 2024-01-15 --end 2024-02-14

# HYCOM, same region/window
python -m driftscope.hycom --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 \
    --start 2025-04-20 --end 2025-06-01 --region "GBM premonsoon"
Both honor cache: re-runs see the file and skip the download. Pass --force to redownload.

title: 10  Currents — CMEMS and HYCOM
text:
11.8 Summary

CMEMS GLORYS at 1/12°, daily, is the default surface current source.
HYCOM ESPC-D-V02 at 1/25° lat is the second source — finer in latitude, beats CMEMS in BoB drifter validation (LW 0.852 vs 0.701).
Both are stored with identical schemas (uo, vo on (time, latitude, longitude)); HYCOM files just carry an _hycom suffix.
The drifter-validation script compares the two side by side; the dynamics-snapshot script defaults to HYCOM for the highest-resolution diagnostics.

Next: the wave and wind data sources from ERA5, and how the Stokes-drift formula in Chapter 8 is computed from them.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12 Waves and winds — ERA5
ECMWF’s ERA5 reanalysis is the global go-to atmospheric record. DriftScope pulls two ERA5 product groups from the Copernicus Climate Data Store:
Both share the same authentication (CDS API key) and the same cadence (6-hourly snapshots). They are the atmospheric terms in Eq. 5.2; everything below the surface comes from CMEMS or HYCOM.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.1 ERA5 in 200 words
ERA5 is the fifth-generation ECMWF reanalysis: 4D-Var assimilation running on the IFS atmospheric model, started in 1940 and continuing with a ~5-day operational lag. Spatial resolution is 0.25° (~25 km at the equator) for atmospheric fields, and 0.5° for wave fields. Temporal cadence is hourly, but DriftScope downloads 6-hourly snapshots (00, 06, 12, 18 UTC) — denser sampling adds little signal for surface drift on multi-day scales.
The reanalysis is documented in Hersbach et al. (2020); for our purposes the key facts are:

It is internally consistent. The wave and wind fields from the same ERA5 run are dynamically coupled. You can mix them.
It is coarser than CMEMS. ERA5 winds at 0.25° barely resolve the Bay of Bengal coastline, much less estuaries. We accept this — wind fields are smoother than ocean fields, and the windage coefficient \(\alpha\) is small enough that a 25-km blur in \(\mathbf{u}_{10}\) doesn’t matter much.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.2 CDS API setup
The Copernicus Climate Data Store requires a free account and an API key. Setup:

Sign up at cds.climate.copernicus.eu.
After login, your API key is on your profile page.
Either set environment variables (preferred for DriftScope):
# in .env
CDSAPI_URL=https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/api
CDSAPI_KEY=12345:abcdef-...
…or create the canonical ~/.cdsapirc:
url: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/api
key: 12345:abcdef-...

DriftScope’s wave and wind fetchers fall back to ~/.cdsapirc if the env vars aren’t set; see driftscope/stokes.py:173.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.3 Waves

12.3.1 What the dataset has
ERA5 reanalysis-era5-single-levels holds a wide menu of wave fields. DriftScope pulls three:

significant_height_of_combined_wind_waves_and_swell (swh, m)
mean_wave_period (mwp, s)
mean_wave_direction (mwd, deg from north, “from”)

These are the minimum to apply Eq. 8.2. A more sophisticated model (3D Stokes drift, depth profile) would need the full directional spectrum — also available in ERA5 but heavier to download and not used by DriftScope yet.


12.3.2 How the fetch works
driftscope/stokes.py:88’s fetch_stokes() fires one cds.retrieve() call per request, asking for the three variables on the bbox/date range:
cds.retrieve(
    "reanalysis-era5-single-levels",
    {
        "product_type": "reanalysis",
        "variable": ["significant_height_of_combined_wind_waves_and_swell",
                     "mean_wave_period", "mean_wave_direction"],
        **_date_lists(start_date, end_date),   # year/month/day as separate lists
        "time": ["00:00", "06:00", "12:00", "18:00"],
        "area": [lat_max, lon_min, lat_min, lon_max],   # CDS uses [N, W, S, E]
        "data_format": "netcdf",
    },
    "raw.nc",
)
CDS queues the request; for a 14-day, 5×5° bbox it typically returns in 30–90 seconds. The result is a netCDF with the three variables on a 0.5° wave grid.
Then we convert to Stokes drift in-place:
ust, vst = stokes_from_waves(ds["swh"], ds["mwp"], ds["mwd"])
ds["ust"], ds["vst"] = ust, vst
ds.to_netcdf(out)
so the saved file holds both the original wave variables (for inspection / replotting) and the derived Stokes components.






Tip



CDS area order is N, W, S, E. Most other clients use lon/lat min/max. Mixing them up gives empty downloads or wrap-around bugs. ERA5’s convention is documented but easy to get wrong; the comment in stokes.py:127 is a cheat sheet.




12.3.3 Output schema
data/waves/<region>_<start>_<end>_waves.nc:
  Variables:
    swh, mwp, mwd      → original ERA5 wave variables
    ust, vst           → derived Stokes drift (m/s)
  Coordinates:
    time (6-hourly)
    latitude  (0.5° spacing)
    longitude (0.5° spacing)
When the simulation runs, combine_forcings() interpolates ust/vst onto the currents grid and adds them. The original wave fields are unused at runtime but useful for plots (“here’s the wave field, here’s the resulting Stokes contribution”).

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.4 Winds
The wind fetcher is structurally identical to the wave fetcher — same ERA5 dataset, same auth, same time grid. Two variables:

10m_u_component_of_wind (u10, m/s eastward)
10m_v_component_of_wind (v10, m/s northward)

driftscope/winds.py:63:
cds.retrieve(
    "reanalysis-era5-single-levels",
    {
        "product_type": "reanalysis",
        "variable": ["10m_u_component_of_wind", "10m_v_component_of_wind"],
        **_date_lists(start_date, end_date),
        "time": ["00:00", "06:00", "12:00", "18:00"],
        "area": [lat_max, lon_min, lat_min, lon_max],
        "data_format": "netcdf",
    },
    "raw.nc",
)

12.4.1 Output
data/winds/<region>_<start>_<end>_winds.nc:
  Variables: u10, v10           → 10 m wind components (m/s)
  Coordinates: time (6-hourly), latitude, longitude (0.25°)
When the simulation runs with --winds, combine_forcings() interpolates u10/v10 onto the currents grid, multiplies by the windage coefficient α, and adds the result to the Eulerian velocity. The full math is in Eq. 8.3.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
section: 12.5 Why we keep waves and winds separate
text:
12.5 Why we keep waves and winds separate
You could imagine fetching them together (one CDS request for five variables). DriftScope keeps them in separate modules because:

Stokes drift is always physically present at the surface; you’d typically want it on. Windage applies only to emergent material (plastic, oil, hull); for fully submerged tracers (SPM at 2 m depth) you turn it off. Different defaults, different toggles.
The conversion logic (stokes_from_waves()) lives with the wave fetcher. If wave-spectrum data became available, it’d live there too without touching winds.
The two modules can be developed and tested independently. The wind fetcher is essentially a one-page module; the wave fetcher has the non-trivial direction-convention math.







Note



Reuse: driftscope/winds.py imports _date_lists from stokes.py (line 45). Both query the same ERA5 catalog, so the date-list builder is shared. This is the only cross-import between them.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.6 Cadence and time alignment
Different forcings live on different time grids:

CMEMS / HYCOM currents: daily
ERA5 waves and winds: 6-hourly
pyTMD tides: hourly (we choose the cadence)

combine_forcings() resolves this by picking the finest time grid present and interpolating coarser fields onto it. If tides are on, output is hourly. If tides are off but waves/winds are on, output is 6-hourly. If only currents, daily.
The simulator’s integration step (default 30 min) is finer than any of these; linear-in-time interpolation between data steps keeps the trajectory smooth.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.7 Lag and availability
ERA5 reanalysis is finalized with a 5-day operational delay. If you ask for “today’s” wave field, the CDS will tell you it’s not available yet. The fetchers default to end_date = today - 6 days to stay safely on the analyzed side.
For runs of current events, you’d switch to ERA5T (preliminary, 1-day lag) or accept the 5-day gap.

title: 11  Waves and winds — ERA5
text:
12.8 Summary

Waves come from ERA5 single-level reanalysis (swh, mwp, mwd) and are converted in-line to Stokes drift via Eq. 8.2.
Winds come from the same ERA5 catalog (u10, v10) and feed the windage term in Eq. 8.3.
Both are stored on a coarser grid than the currents (0.25–0.5°). The simulation’s combine step interpolates them onto the currents grid before integration.
Both share the CDS API authentication. One key, two modules.

Next: tides, the trickiest data source — not because of the model, but because of pyTMD 3.x’s API.




Hersbach, H., Bell, B., Berrisford, P., et al. (2020). The ERA5 global reanalysis. Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, 146(730), 1999–2049. https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.3803

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13 Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
Chapter 8 explained why tides matter and what harmonic prediction does. This chapter is about the implementation — the TPXO9 model, the pyTMD library that queries it, and the seven gotchas DriftScope navigated when wiring it up.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.1 TPXO9-atlas-v5
The TPXO project at Oregon State publishes a series of global tide models constrained by altimetry and tide gauges. TPXO9-atlas-v5 is a regionally-refined product that combines:

A base 1/6° global grid (TPXO9-atlas).
High-resolution 1/30° local grids over major coastlines (including the Bay of Bengal).

The high-res patches stitch into the base grid — when you query a location in a high-res region, you get 1/30° values; outside, you get 1/6°. For the Sundarbans, the local grid resolves the tidal amplification in the delta channels surprisingly well given the simple harmonic representation.
The model has 13 constituents: the major semidiurnals (\(M_2\), \(S_2\), \(N_2\), \(K_2\)), diurnals (\(K_1\), \(O_1\), \(P_1\), \(Q_1\)), long-period (\(M_f\), \(M_m\)), and shallow-water nonlinear terms (\(M_4\), \(M_8\), \(MS_4\)). For deep-water and shelf regions the four largest (\(M_2\), \(S_2\), \(K_1\), \(O_1\)) account for >90% of the tidal variance.






Tip



Why “atlas” and “v5”? The “atlas” refers to the local-grid stitching (it’s a map, not just a global field). “v5” is the model version — each release retunes the inversion against newer altimetry. As of 2026-05, v5 (released 2024) is current.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.2 How to get TPXO9
The TPXO model is freely distributed but requires registration. Setup:

Register at tpxo.net.
Approval is manual; takes ~24 h.
Download TPXO9-atlas-v5 (NetCDF) from the link in the approval email. ~1 GB.
Unpack to a local directory. Set TIDE_MODEL_DIR in .env to point at it.

DriftScope verifies the path on import:
# driftscope/tides.py:56
def _check_model() -> Path:
    model_dir = os.getenv("TIDE_MODEL_DIR")
    if not model_dir:
        raise RuntimeError("TIDE_MODEL_DIR not set in .env. ...")
    p = Path(model_dir).expanduser()
    if not p.exists():
        raise RuntimeError(f"TIDE_MODEL_DIR points to non-existent path: {p}")
    return p
If you skip TPXO setup, all tide-related calls raise this RuntimeError with a setup hint. The rest of the pipeline (currents, waves, etc.) still works.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.3 pyTMD — the prediction library
pyTMD is the Python re-implementation of the OSU Matlab tide-prediction routines, maintained by NSIDC. It reads TPXO (and FES, OTIS, GOT) files and predicts tidal currents and heights at any lat/lon/time.
DriftScope wraps pyTMD.compute.tide_currents() in driftscope/tides.py:121:
res = pyTMD.compute.tide_currents(
    xx, yy, tt, component="u",
    directory=str(model_dir),
    model="TPXO9-atlas-v5-nc",
    epoch=(2000, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0),
    type="drift",
    standard="UTC",
    crs=4326,
    method="linear",
    extrapolate=False,
    fill_value=np.nan,
    crop=True,
    bounds=bounds,
    buffer=1.0,
)

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.4 The seven gotchas
pyTMD 3.x has a handful of API quirks that aren’t obviously documented. The seven the project navigated:

Kwargs are case-sensitive in unexpected places. directory= works, Directory= doesn’t.
tide_currents() is the right function name (not tide_velocity or predict_currents). Older docs reference different names.
Model name must include -nc suffix for the NetCDF distribution: "TPXO9-atlas-v5-nc", not "TPXO9-atlas-v5".
directory should be the parent of the unpacked model, not the model dir itself. pyTMD looks for Model_*.txt files in there.
bounds ordering is [xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax], not the more common [lon_min, lat_min, lon_max, lat_max]. Quietly wrong if you mismatch.
The return value is an xarray.DataTree (with branches per component), not a plain Dataset. Convert with .to_dataset().
Output units are cm/s, not m/s. Multiply by 0.01.

That last one is the easiest to forget — DriftScope does it explicitly in tides.py:139:
u_flat = np.nan_to_num(np.asarray(ds.u.values), nan=0.0) * 0.01
v_flat = np.nan_to_num(np.asarray(ds.v.values), nan=0.0) * 0.01






Warning



Don’t filter NaN early. nan_to_num(..., nan=0.0) zeros out land cells. Without this, the combined u_currents + u_tide becomes NaN over land cells where \(u_\text{tide}\) is undefined, and the integrator’s land mask gets confused. We zero land tides; the simulator’s separate land mask removes particles that drift onto land anyway.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.5 Output schema
driftscope/tides.py:193 writes:
data/tides/<region>_<start>_<end>_tides.nc:
  Variables: u_tide, v_tide        (m/s)
  Coordinates:
    time      hourly (default; configurable via TIDE_DT_HOURS)
    latitude  inherited from currents grid
    longitude inherited from currents grid
The grid is identical to the currents file’s grid. This is by design — the simulation’s combine step doesn’t have to interpolate spatially when adding tides to currents, just temporally.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
section: 13.6 How tides change the time grid
text:
13.6 How tides change the time grid
When you turn on tides, the simulation’s combined forcing NetCDF is re-gridded onto the tides’ hourly time axis. Daily currents are forward-filled to each hour. See simulate.py:91:
if tides_nc is not None:
    tid = xr.open_dataset(tides_nc)
    time_grid = tid["time"]
    cur_resampled = cur.reindex(time=time_grid, method="nearest")
else:
    time_grid = cur["time"]
    cur_resampled = cur
This is the right thing: M2 has a 12.42-hour period, which would alias horribly on a daily grid. The simulator’s 30-min integration step then samples the hourly tide curve smoothly via linear-in-time interpolation between hours.






Tip



Tide-aware time stepping. Without tides, \(\Delta t = 30\) min is overkill — you could go to 1 h with no loss. With tides on, 30 min is already at the edge of what cleanly resolves M2. Don’t extend \(\Delta t\) beyond 30 min when tides are active.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.7 Sanity-check the output
Quick visual: pick a point in the bbox and plot \(u_\text{tide}(t)\) for a day:
import xarray as xr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ds = xr.open_dataset("data/tides/sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01_tides.nc")
ts = ds.u_tide.sel(longitude=89.0, latitude=21.4, method="nearest")
ts.plot()
plt.savefig("tide_check.png")
You should see:

A near-pure sinusoid with 12.4-hour period (M2 dominates in the BoB).
Spring/neap modulation if you plot >2 weeks.
Amplitude 0.3–1.5 m/s depending on location (offshore < shelf < delta channels).

If you see no signal, your TIDE_MODEL_DIR is probably wrong, or crop=True accidentally cropped your bbox out.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.8 Why not FES or GOT?
pyTMD also supports FES2014 and GOT4.10. They are alternative global tide models constrained by similar altimetry data. For most ocean applications they perform within 5% of TPXO9 in mid-latitudes. We default to TPXO9 because:

It has the densest local-grid coverage in the Bay of Bengal.
It’s what the Lenain et al. (2026) GOFLOW paper benchmarks against, so cross-comparison with submesoscale work is direct.
The 13 constituents are sufficient for shelf work; FES has 34 but the extras are second-order.

You can swap models by changing TIDE_MODEL_NAME in driftscope/config.py:139. The rest of the pipeline doesn’t care.

title: 12  Tides — TPXO9 via pyTMD
text:
13.9 Summary

TPXO9-atlas-v5 is the default tide model — 1/6° global with 1/30° refinement over coastlines, 13 harmonic constituents.
pyTMD does the harmonic prediction; DriftScope wraps it with seven workarounds for API quirks.
Output is on the currents grid spatially at hourly cadence; the simulation’s time grid switches to hourly when tides are on.
Setup requires a one-time TPXO download (~1 GB) and TIDE_MODEL_DIR in .env.

Next: the observation-channel datasets — SST, chlorophyll, drifters, and SPM — that we use for context, validation, and (in Module 7) initial conditions.




Lenain, L. et al. (2026). GOFLOW: Geostationary ocean flow. Nature Geoscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-01943-0

title: 13  Observations — SST, chlorophyll, drifters
text:
14 Observations — SST, chlorophyll, drifters
The currents/wave/wind/tide datasets are forcings — they drive the simulation. The datasets in this chapter are observations — used for context (does the simulated plume align with the chlorophyll feature?), validation (does a real GDP drifter follow the simulated track?), or, in Module 7, initial conditions (where is sediment in the water now?).
All three are CMEMS-distributed (except drifters, from NOAA AOML), and all three need only the same CMEMS auth as currents (or no auth, for drifters).

title: 13  Observations — SST, chlorophyll, drifters
text:
14.1 OSTIA L4 SST
The UK Met Office’s OSTIA (Operational Sea Surface Temperature and Sea Ice Analysis) is a daily, gap-filled, multi-sensor SST analysis. CMEMS distributes it as METOFFICE-GLO-SST-L4-NRT-OBS-SST-V2.

L4 means “gap-filled and merged” — no clouds, no orbital tracks, one number per cell.
5 km global resolution.
Inputs: AVHRR, AMSR2, VIIRS, in-situ — fused via optimal interpolation.

For DriftScope, SST plays two roles:

Front detection. \(\log_{10}|\nabla T|\) at OSTIA’s 5 km resolution reveals frontal structure that smoothed daily-mean velocity products miss. Used in the dynamics-snapshot figure (Chapter 20).
Sanity check on currents. Eddies show up as cold (cyclonic) or warm (anticyclonic) cores in SST. If your simulated current map shows an eddy where SST shows nothing, one of them is wrong — usually the currents (resolution).

driftscope/sst.py:51 is a one-call CMEMS subset:
copernicusmarine.subset(
    dataset_id="METOFFICE-GLO-SST-L4-NRT-OBS-SST-V2",
    variables=["analysed_sst"],   # Kelvin
    minimum_longitude=lon_min, ..., maximum_latitude=lat_max,
    start_datetime=..., end_datetime=...,
    output_filename=..., output_directory=...,
)
Output:
data/sst/<region>_<start>_<end>_sst.nc:
  Variables: analysed_sst         (Kelvin)
  Coordinates: time, latitude, longitude (0.05°)






Tip



SST is in Kelvin, not Celsius. OSTIA’s analysed_sst is in K, and the units attribute says so. Subtract 273.15 to plot in °C — the dynamics-snapshot script does this explicitly. If you forget, your colorbar shows “300 K” and you wonder why the ocean is on fire.

title: 13  Observations — SST, chlorophyll, drifters
text:
14.2 Chlorophyll-a (Ocean Color CCI)
driftscope/chlorophyll.py downloads the CMEMS multi-sensor merged chlorophyll-a (cmems_obs-oc_glo_bgc-plankton_my_l4-multi-4km_P1D).

Inputs: MODIS Aqua/Terra, VIIRS-SNPP, OLCI-A/B (Sentinel-3).
4 km global resolution.
MY (multi-year reanalysis) covers 1997–present with ~6-month lag.
NRT (near-real-time) covers the last ~30 days.

Chlorophyll is useful for biological context — river plumes carry nutrients that drive coastal blooms. A trajectory that ends up in a high- chlorophyll patch is consistent with the river-runoff release; one that ends in oligotrophic open water has dispersed beyond the productive zone. The chlorophyll field doesn’t go into the simulation but it helps interpret the output.
Output:
data/chlorophyll/<region>_<start>_<end>_chl.nc:
  Variables: CHL                  (mg m⁻³)
  Coordinates: time, latitude, longitude (4 km)






Warning



Cloud cover dominates daily chlorophyll. Even at L4, gaps from persistent monsoon clouds leave large white patches. Use 8-day or monthly composites for analysis (CMEMS provides those too); daily L4 is mostly useful for individual-event synoptic plots.

title: 13  Observations — SST, chlorophyll, drifters
text:
14.3 Global Drifter Program drifters
Real surface drifters drogued at 15 m, GPS-tracked, quality-controlled by NOAA AOML. The most credible single validation source for a Lagrangian model.
The drifter program archives ~30,000 drifter histories from the 1980s to today. We pull regional subsets via NOAA AOML’s ERDDAP server, which speaks plain HTTP and returns CSV — no auth required.
driftscope/drifters.py:52 builds a URL like:
https://erddap.aoml.noaa.gov/gdp/erddap/tabledap/drifter_hourly_qc.csv
?ID,time,latitude,longitude
&time%3E=2025-04-20T00:00:00Z
&time%3C=2025-06-01T23:59:59Z
&latitude%3E=19
&latitude%3C=23
&longitude%3E=87.5
&longitude%3C=92.5
(%3E= is URL-encoded >=, %3C= is <=.) The response is a CSV that pandas reads directly:
df = pd.read_csv(url, skiprows=[1])   # row 1 is units, skip
df = df.rename(columns={"latitude": "lat", "longitude": "lon"})
df["time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["time"])
Output:
data/drifters/<region>_<start>_<end>_drifters.csv:
  Columns: ID, time, lat, lon
Each ID is one drifter’s full hourly track within the bbox/time window.






Tip



Empty CSV is a valid result. The Bay of Bengal sees 0–5 active drifters in a typical month. If the URL returns no rows, ERDDAP responds with HTTP 404 (not 200 + empty body). The fetcher catches this and writes an empty CSV with the right headers, so the cache check still works on re-run.



14.3.1 Why GDP for validation
The drifter is drogued at 15 m. It tracks the 15-m current — close to the surface but not the very surface. CMEMS at 0.494 m and HYCOM at its surface level are also near-surface but not at 15 m. So a CMEMS-vs-drifter comparison has a 15-m model–data offset built in. In practice this is small (0.1° amplitude) compared to the 1/12° gridding error.
For a more rigorous validation, you’d want un-drogued drifters (they ride the very surface) — but those are noisier (windage matters) and there are far fewer in the BoB record.
The validation chapter (Chapter 19) walks through:

Fetching one specific GDP drifter’s track.
Running a DriftScope simulation seeded at the drifter’s release point/time.
Computing the Liu–Weisberg skill score — a normalized error metric where 1.0 is perfect, 0.0 is “no skill better than zero velocity”, and >0.5 is generally usable.

text:
14.4 Convention: where data lives
All three observation modules write to typed subdirectories under data/:
data/sst/         OSTIA L4 SST netCDFs
data/chlorophyll/ Ocean Color CCI L4 netCDFs
data/drifters/    GDP CSVs
Filenames follow the same <region>_<start>_<end>_<kind>.{nc,csv} convention as currents and tides. This pattern is set in driftscope/config.py:13’s path constants and reused by every fetcher.

title: 13  Observations — SST, chlorophyll, drifters
text:
14.5 Summary

OSTIA L4 SST at 5 km, daily, gap-filled — for fronts, eddies, and the dynamics-snapshot figure.
CCI chlorophyll-a at 4 km, daily, multi-sensor merged — for biological context.
GDP drifters at hourly cadence — for validation against real Lagrangian particles.
All share the deterministic <region>_<start>_<end>_<kind> filename convention.

Next: SPM, the Module 7 satellite-derived sediment retrieval that provides initial conditions for sediment-transport simulations.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
text:
15 SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM) is the sediment-transport module — Module 7 in the project roadmap. Unlike the forcing modules (Chapter 11 through Chapter 13) which provide velocity fields, and unlike the observation modules (Chapter 14) which provide context for validation, SPM provides initial conditions: “where is the sediment in the water right now?”
The retrieval algorithm is cluster-based regression (CBR), following Geyman & Maloof (2019), who originally developed it for bathymetry on the Great Bahama Bank. We adapt the same structure to SPM concentration in the optically-heterogeneous Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
text:
15.1 What SPM is, optically
Multispectral satellite imagery (Sentinel-2, Landsat) measures water-leaving reflectance at several visible/near-infrared bands. Suspended sediment in the upper few meters scatters light — adds reflectance in the green/red, saturates in the NIR. The observed reflectance vector at each pixel is a function of:

SPM concentration (mg/L) — what we want to recover.
Phytoplankton chlorophyll — adds green absorption.
Colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) — adds blue absorption.
Bottom reflectance in shallow water.
Atmospheric residuals in coastal scenes (adjacency to bright land).

In the open ocean, SPM ↔︎ reflectance is monotonic and a single global regression works. In the GBM delta, water types vary radically over a few kilometers:

River-plume water: very high SPM (50–500 mg/L), low chlorophyll, high CDOM.
Mixing zone: intermediate SPM, mid-CDOM.
Shelf-marine: low SPM (<10 mg/L), variable chlorophyll, low CDOM.
CDOM-rich tributary: low SPM, very high CDOM (Sundarbans channels).

Each has a different SPM-vs-reflectance shape. A single global fit averages across all four and biases each.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
section: 15.2 The CBR idea, step by step
text:
15.2 The CBR idea, step by step
CBR partitions the image spectrally first, then fits a regression per cluster:

Cluster the per-pixel reflectance vectors into \(k\) classes (k-means on the band space, \(k = 4\) for the GBM delta).
For each class, fit a regression SPM($R_1, R_2, …) using matchup data points whose reflectance vectors are near that class centroid.
At inference time on a new pixel, don’t pick one class — compute the spectral distance to every centroid and blend the \(k\) predictions weighted by \(1/d_i\).

The blending step is what makes CBR robust: a pixel exactly between plume and mixing-zone water gets a weighted average of the two class-specific regressions, rather than a hard switch.






Tip



Why not SVM or random forest? Both work, but they lose physical interpretability. CBR’s per-class regression is log-linear in the band ratios, which is the form physical theory predicts (Nechad et al. 2010, semi-analytical SPM). When calibration data are sparse — always the case in remote estuaries — physically structured models extrapolate gracefully where black-box ML over-fits the matchups.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
text:
15.3 What’s implemented
The CBR algorithm itself is complete in driftscope/spm.py — pure NumPy + scikit-learn. A smoke test demonstrates CBR successfully recovering two known water-type relationships from synthetic data.
The two upstream pieces are stubbed (not yet wired):

Sentinel-2 fetch: a function that pulls Sentinel-2 L2A reflectance for a bbox/date through Microsoft’s Planetary Computer STAC. The PR is open; needs auth and storage settings.
Matchup ingest: a loader that pulls the AquaMatch v2 TSS measurements (in-situ SPM, 1.4 M observations, US-only) and the matched SiteSR Landsat reflectances. This is a 50 GB download distributed across nine .feather files. Helper at driftscope/aquamatch.py.

The CBR algorithm runs on either source: synthetic data for testing, real matchups for production. Calibration on US estuaries and application to BoB scenes is the transfer-learning pattern — following Tian et al. (2026)’s pan-Arctic SSC work, which calibrated on US sites and applied to Arctic deltas.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
text:
15.4 Atmospheric correction
Sentinel-2 L2A products are atmospherically corrected by ESA’s Sen2Cor algorithm. For a quick-look CBR retrieval this is acceptable — the per-class regression absorbs whatever residual atmospheric bias is uniform within a class, since clusters are determined by the data.
For production-grade SPM retrieval — especially in the Sundarbans where mangrove canopy adjacent to dark water creates strong adjacency effects — upgrade to ACOLITE, an aquatic-specialized atmospheric corrector that handles sun glint, aerosol mixtures, and adjacency Vanhellemont & Ruddick (2018). Requires Sentinel-2 L1C (top-of-atmosphere) inputs instead of L2A; adds ~30 min/scene of local processing.
The CBR algorithm doesn’t care which AC was applied — its inputs are just reflectance vectors. Swapping AC pipelines changes the calibration weights but not the algorithm.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
section: 15.5 How the SPM map enters a simulation
text:
15.5 How the SPM map enters a simulation
scripts/run_coupled_simulation.py demonstrates the SPM-weighted release: instead of seeding particles in a uniform disk or basin fill, you sample release locations with probability proportional to local SPM concentration.
# scripts/run_coupled_simulation.py:52
def sample_spm_weighted_seeds(spm_nc, currents_nc, n, rng,
                              min_spm_mg_l=5.0):
    spm = xr.open_dataset(spm_nc).load().spm_mg_l
    cur = xr.open_dataset(currents_nc).load()
    u0 = cur.uo.isel(time=0).squeeze()

    w = spm.values.astype(float)
    valid = np.isfinite(w) & (w > min_spm_mg_l)
    w = np.where(valid, w, 0.0)

    flat_w = w.ravel() / w.sum()
    idx = rng.choice(n_pix, size=n_cand, replace=True, p=flat_w)
    lat_idx, lon_idx = np.unravel_index(idx, w.shape)
    plat = spm.latitude.values[lat_idx]
    plon = spm.longitude.values[lon_idx]
    ...
    return plon, plat
The result: 2000 particles seeded preferentially where the satellite saw sediment, then advected with all forcings (currents + tides + waves + wind + Brownian + settling). The dispersion plot shows where that sediment goes over the next ten days.






Tip



Time-aligned vs representative initial conditions. DriftScope’s demo uses a 2024-03-08 (dry-season) SPM map as the release pattern even when the simulation runs through 2026-04-17 — using the SPM map as a spatial release pattern, not as a time-aligned tracer concentration. For temporally-aligned runs you’d need a Sentinel-2 scene from the simulation start date. Once Module 7’s fetch is wired up, this becomes a one-line change.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
section: 15.6 What you’d do as a student
text:
15.6 What you’d do as a student
Three Module-7 exercises that pay back the most:

Run CBR on synthetic data to see the algorithm work end-to-end. The smoke test in driftscope/spm.py produces a side-by-side “true vs retrieved” map and an error histogram.
Compute the SPM-weighted release on the existing 2024-03-08 map and run a 10-day simulation with all forcings. Compare the final particle positions with a same-period chlorophyll map — high SPM should track the river-plume signal.
Plug a real matchup dataset in (US sites for now) and check that the per-class regressions recover (Nechad et al., 2010)-style band-ratio shapes — a sanity check that the algorithm is finding the physics, not memorizing the data.

title: 14  SPM — Sentinel-2 + cluster-based regression
text:
15.7 Summary

SPM is a satellite-derived initial-condition map for sediment transport, not a forcing field.
The retrieval algorithm is cluster-based regression, suited to optically heterogeneous deltas — a single global regression systematically biases each water type.
The CBR algorithm is complete in driftscope/spm.py; the upstream Sentinel-2 fetch and matchup ingest are stubs.
Used in the coupled simulation to seed particles where the sediment actually is rather than uniformly.
See scripts/spm_apply_sundarbans.py for a worked example.

This closes out the Data part of the book. The next part is the module reference — a one-page-per-file map of the codebase, plus short notes on viz.py and animate.py that haven’t earned their own chapters.

Nechad, B., Ruddick, K. G., & Park, Y. (2010). Calibration and validation of a generic multisensor algorithm for mapping of total suspended matter in turbid waters. Remote Sensing of Environment, 114(4), 854–866. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2009.11.022

title: 15  Module reference
text:
16 Module reference
A one-screen map of every file in driftscope/, what it does, where you’d touch it. Sized to be skimmable; depth lives in the chapters above.

title: 15  Module reference
text:
16.1 Configuration & shared state

16.1.1 config.py — 178 lines
Defines Region, SimConfig, PRESETS, dataset IDs, file-system paths. Touch when: adding a new region, changing a default parameter, or switching dataset versions. Imported by every other module.
Key objects:








Name
Type
Purpose




PRESETS
dict[str, Region]
Named bboxes — sundarbans, hooghly_mouth, bay_of_bengal, etc.


SimConfig
dataclass
All knobs for a simulation run (particles, runtime, forcings, settling, Brownian)


CMEMS_DATASET_ID, ERA5_DATASET, TIDE_MODEL_NAME, etc.
string constants
Dataset IDs used by fetchers — single point of change for product upgrades


CURRENTS_DIR, WAVES_DIR, …, TRAJ_DIR
Path constants
Auto-created on import; never mkdir manually

title: 15  Module reference
text:
16.2 Data fetchers

16.2.1 fetch.py — 143 lines
Downloads CMEMS surface currents. One function, fetch_currents(), called via python -m driftscope.fetch.


16.2.2 hycom.py — 174 lines
Downloads HYCOM ESPC-D-V02 surface currents via OPeNDAP byte-range subsetting. Output schema deliberately matches fetch.py so they’re interchangeable downstream. CLI: python -m driftscope.hycom.


16.2.3 stokes.py — 185 lines
Downloads ERA5 wave parameters (\(H_s\), \(T_m\), mwd) and computes Stokes drift in-place via stokes_from_waves(). Output has both raw wave fields and derived \(u_\text{st}, v_\text{st}\). CLI: python -m driftscope.stokes.


16.2.4 winds.py — 147 lines
Downloads ERA5 10 m winds (\(u_{10}, v_{10}\)). Reuses _date_lists from stokes.py since both query the same ERA5 catalog. CLI: python -m driftscope.winds.


16.2.5 tides.py — 245 lines
Predicts tidal currents from TPXO9-atlas-v5 via pyTMD. Most logic is the seven workarounds for pyTMD 3.x quirks (Chapter 13). Requires TIDE_MODEL_DIR in .env. CLI: python -m driftscope.tides.


16.2.6 sst.py — 120 lines
Downloads OSTIA L4 SST (Kelvin) via CMEMS. CLI: python -m driftscope.sst.


16.2.7 chlorophyll.py — 126 lines
Downloads Ocean Color CCI L4 chlorophyll-a (mg/m³) via CMEMS. CLI: python -m driftscope.chlorophyll.


16.2.8 drifters.py — 152 lines
Pulls GDP drifter tracks (CSV) from NOAA AOML’s ERDDAP. No auth required. CLI: python -m driftscope.drifters.


16.2.9 rivers.py — 92 lines
Helpers for Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna river-discharge climatology used in seasonal-comparison runs. Loads monthly mean discharge by river and exposes seasonal_label() for plot titling.


16.2.10 spm.py — 885 lines
Module 7: cluster-based regression for satellite-derived SPM. Pure NumPy + sklearn. CBR algorithm is complete; Sentinel-2 fetch and matchup ingest are stubbed. See Chapter 15.


16.2.11 aquamatch.py — 268 lines
Helpers for the AquaMatch v2 in-situ TSS + SiteSR Landsat reflectance matchup dataset (50 GB across nine .feather files). Used to train CBR on US estuaries; transferred to BoB scenes following Tian 2026’s pan-Arctic recipe.

title: 15  Module reference
text:
16.3 Simulation core

16.3.1 simulate.py — 467 lines
The run loop. Three layers:

combine_forcings() (line 47): build a single combined velocity NetCDF from CMEMS/HYCOM + Stokes + tides + winds.
seed_disk() and seeding logic (lines 156–331): build the particle release cloud — disk, basin-fill, or caller-supplied (e.g. SPM-weighted).
run_simulation() (line 165): hand the FieldSet to OceanParcels and execute the kernel chain.

Touch when: adding a new forcing (extend combine_forcings), changing the seeding pattern, or wiring a new kernel.


16.3.2 kernels.py — 147 lines
OceanParcels kernels:

stokes_settling_velocity() — Stokes’ law, returns m/s.
AdvectionRK4_Land() — RK4 with friendly land deletion.
Settling() — vertical advection by per-particle w_settle.
BrownianMotion2D() — sub-grid diffusion random walk.

Plus stubs for StokesDrift, Windage, etc., showing the pattern for adding a new kernel.

title: 15  Module reference
text:
16.4 Diagnostics & visualization

16.4.1 diagnostics.py — 167 lines
Eulerian diagnostics — the same fields the GOFLOW figure shows: speed, \(\log|\nabla V|\), \(\zeta/f\), \(\delta/f\). Pure NumPy plus a plot_diagnostics() 2×2 panel renderer. The new scripts/sundarban_dynamics_snapshot.py extends this with a velocity-over-SST panel and an inset speed time-series.


16.4.2 viz.py — 113 lines
Trajectory-plot helpers:

load_trajectories(zarr_path) — open a Zarr trajectory archive.
traj_to_dataframe(ds) — flatten to a long-form pandas DataFrame (traj, time, lon, lat).
plot_traj(...) — matplotlib scatter with time-coloring.



16.4.3 animate.py — 238 lines
Frame-by-frame matplotlib animations — particle trails over a time-evolving velocity field. Used by the seasonal-comparison script (Chapter 21) to produce the GBM monsoon-vs-dry 4-panel comparison and the per-season standalone GIFs.

Each one is a standalone end-to-end pipeline that uses the modules. Touch them to do science; touch the modules to change capabilities.

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17 Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
Goal: run a CMEMS-only Lagrangian simulation in the Sundarbans, plot the trajectories, understand every parameter you set. ~20 minutes from the quickstart end-state.

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.1 Step 0 — preconditions
Assumes you’ve done Chapter 3 and have:

conda activate driftscope
.env with valid CMEMS credentials.
A working python -c "import parcels, copernicusmarine".

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.2 Step 1 — fetch currents
python -m driftscope.fetch \
    --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 \
    --start 2025-01-15 --end 2025-01-29 \
    --region sundarbans
This pulls 14 days of CMEMS daily-mean surface currents. Output: data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc. ~600 KB.






Tip



Why these dates? Mid-January 2025 is dry season: no monsoon freshening, no spring tropical cyclone, mostly weak coastal currents under NE monsoon winds. A clean baseline. We’ll reuse this to compare seasons later.

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.3 Step 2 — run a basic simulation
python -m driftscope.simulate \
    --currents data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc \
    --particles 500 \
    --days 10 \
    --seed-lon 89.0 \
    --seed-lat 21.2 \
    --seed-radius 0.15
What you just configured:



Flag
Meaning




--currents
Use this specific NetCDF (overrides “latest in dir”)


--particles 500
Release 500 particles


--days 10
Integrate for 10 days


--seed-lon, --seed-lat
Center of the disk-shaped release


--seed-radius 0.15
Disk radius in degrees ≈ 16 km



Default dt is 30 min (RK4); default save cadence is 3 h. So you’ll get 81 saved time steps × 500 particles = 40,500 position records.
Output: data/trajectories/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29__currents_only_traj.zarr/.
The console will print something like:
· loading currents: sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc
· seeded 500/500 particles at (89.000, 21.200) r=0.15°
→ running 10d, dt=30min, save every 180min
INFO: Compiled JITKernel ...
100% ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 240/240 0:00:33
✓ trajectories: data/trajectories/...

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.4 Step 3 — open the trajectories
import xarray as xr
from driftscope.viz import load_trajectories, traj_to_dataframe

ds = load_trajectories(
    "data/trajectories/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29__currents_only_traj.zarr"
)
df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
print(df.head())
print(f"\n{df['traj'].nunique()} particles, "
      f"{df['time'].nunique()} time steps, "
      f"{len(df):,} total rows")
Output:
   traj                time     lon     lat
0     0 2025-01-15 00:00:00  89.020  21.193
1     0 2025-01-15 03:00:00  89.018  21.198
...
500 particles, 81 time steps, 40,500 total rows

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.5 Step 4 — three plots
Each one shows the run from a different angle. Run all three; together they’re a good first impression.

17.5.1 Plot 1: trajectory bundle
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))

for traj_id, group in df.groupby("traj"):
    ax.plot(group.lon, group.lat, alpha=0.15, lw=0.6, color="navy")

# Release point and final positions
first = df.groupby("traj").head(1)
last = df.groupby("traj").tail(1)
ax.scatter(first.lon, first.lat, c="green", s=8, label="release")
ax.scatter(last.lon, last.lat, c="red", s=8, label="day 10")
ax.set_xlim(88.0, 90.5); ax.set_ylim(21.0, 22.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)"); ax.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")
ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Dry-season Sundarbans drift, 10 days, CMEMS only")
plt.savefig("data/tutorial1_trajectories.png", dpi=150,
            bbox_inches="tight")
What to look for:

Direction: which way did particles go on average? In dry season the dominant flow is south-southwest (Indian winter coastal current).
Spread: how broad is the cloud at day 10? A coherent flow produces a tight cloud; a sheared flow produces a broad smear.



17.5.2 Plot 2: time-coloured scatter
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
sc = ax.scatter(df.lon, df.lat, c=df.time.astype('int64'),
                cmap='magma', s=1.5, alpha=0.4)
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label='time')
ax.set_xlim(88.0, 90.5); ax.set_ylim(21.0, 22.8)
ax.set_title("Time-coloured particle positions, days 0–10")
plt.savefig("data/tutorial1_time_scatter.png", dpi=150,
            bbox_inches="tight")
The colorbar maps numerical time to color; dark = release, bright = day 10. Useful for spotting slow-vs-fast lobes within the cloud.


17.5.3 Plot 3: final-position heatmap
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

last = df.groupby("traj").tail(1)
H, xedges, yedges = np.histogram2d(
    last.lon, last.lat,
    bins=[40, 40], range=[[88, 90.5], [21, 22.8]],
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
im = ax.imshow(H.T, origin='lower', cmap='magma', aspect='auto',
               extent=[88, 90.5, 21, 22.8])
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label='# particles in cell')
ax.set_title("Final particle density at day 10")
plt.savefig("data/tutorial1_density.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
This is the operational answer: “if I released 500 particles here, where would they be 10 days later?” The heatmap binds 1:1 to a real-world question.

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.6 What you’ve shown
Three things, by demonstration:

CMEMS-driven drift in the Sundarbans is steady but slow. Daily means smooth out the 12-h tidal oscillation; the residual is the wind-driven Ekman current.
Even in 10 days with no random noise, dispersion happens. This is the shear-driven dispersion of Chapter 10. The cloud spreads because different particles sample slightly different velocities along the way.
A 500-particle ensemble is enough to see the structure clearly. Going to 5,000 would reveal more cloud detail; 50 would be noisy. Pick a number that shows the answer without burning compute.

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.7 What’s missing
Compare what you just did with the master equation Eq. 5.2:
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt} = \mathbf{u}_\text{currents} + \underbrace{\mathbf{u}_\text{Stokes}}_{\text{missing}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{u}_\text{tides}}_{\text{missing}} + \underbrace{\alpha\,\mathbf{u}_{10}}_{\text{missing}} + \mathbf{w}_\text{settle} + \boldsymbol{\eta}_t
\]
You’ve used only \(\mathbf{u}_\text{currents}\). The other four velocity terms are zero. For the Sundarbans this is a bad approximation — tides dominate the shelf flow, and you’re missing a huge piece of the truth.
The next tutorial puts them all in.

title: 16  Tutorial 1 — Your first simulation
text:
17.8 Try it: change one thing






Note



Try it — five-minute exercise. Re-run with --seed-mode bbox and --particles 2000. This switches from a small disk release to a “basin fill” — particles uniformly across all ocean cells. The trajectory bundle becomes a coastline-shaped sheet of particles, and you’ll see the coastal current as a coherent flow along the shelf break. This is one of the most useful release modes for “where does sediment from the shelf go?” questions.


Continue to Chapter 18 to add tides, waves, wind, settling, and Brownian noise — the full master equation.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18 Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
Goal: run the same Sundarbans setup as Tutorial 1 but with the full master equation. Compare with-vs-without each forcing to see what each term contributes. ~45 minutes including downloads.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18.1 Step 0 — preconditions

data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc already exists from Tutorial 1. (If not, fetch it first.)
.env has CDSAPI_KEY for ERA5 (waves and winds).
Optionally, TIDE_MODEL_DIR for tides; this tutorial works without tides but is more interesting with them.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18.2 Step 1 — fetch the additional forcings
# Waves (ERA5; ~30 s)
python -m driftscope.stokes \
    --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 \
    --start 2025-01-15 --end 2025-01-29 \
    --region sundarbans

# Winds (ERA5; ~30 s)
python -m driftscope.winds \
    --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 \
    --start 2025-01-15 --end 2025-01-29 \
    --region sundarbans

# Tides (pyTMD; instant after one-time TPXO setup)
python -m driftscope.tides \
    --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 \
    --start 2025-01-15 --end 2025-01-29 \
    --region sundarbans
You now have:
data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc
data/waves/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_waves.nc
data/winds/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_winds.nc
data/tides/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_tides.nc






Note



Skip tides: if you don’t have TPXO, drop the --tides flag below. The simulation runs fine without; you just lose the dominant signal in shelf regions.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18.3 Step 2 — run the coupled simulation
python -m driftscope.simulate \
    --currents data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc \
    --particles 500 \
    --days 10 \
    --seed-lon 89.0 --seed-lat 21.2 --seed-radius 0.15 \
    --stokes data/waves/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_waves.nc \
    --tides data/tides/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_tides.nc \
    --winds data/winds/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_winds.nc \
    --windage 0.02 \
    --settle --settle-diameter-um 10
What’s new:



Flag
Adds




--stokes <file>
Stokes drift from ERA5 waves


--tides <file>
Barotropic tides from TPXO9


--winds <file>

--windage 0.02
2% — typical for sediment-laden water


--settle
Enable Stokes settling (Module 5)


--settle-diameter-um 10
10 µm silt-class quartz



Console output (truncated):
· forcings: currents + Stokes×1.0 + tides + wind×2.0%
· settling: 10.0µm @ 2650 kg/m³ → w_s = 0.0905 mm/s (7.82 m/day)
· loading currents: sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29__stokes1.0_tides_wind2.0pct.nc
· seeded 500/500 particles at (89.000, 21.200) r=0.15°
→ running 10d, dt=30min, save every 180min

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18.4 Step 3 — overlay vs Tutorial 1
import xarray as xr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from driftscope.viz import load_trajectories, traj_to_dataframe

# CMEMS-only baseline from Tutorial 1
ds_basic = load_trajectories(
    "data/trajectories/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29__currents_only_traj.zarr"
)
df_basic = traj_to_dataframe(ds_basic)

# Coupled run
ds_coup = load_trajectories(
    "data/trajectories/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29"
    "__stokes1.0_tides_wind2.0pct__settle10um_traj.zarr"
)
df_coup = traj_to_dataframe(ds_coup)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))

# Tutorial 1: faint
for tid, grp in df_basic.groupby("traj"):
    ax.plot(grp.lon, grp.lat, color="steelblue", lw=0.5, alpha=0.10)
last_basic = df_basic.groupby("traj").tail(1)
ax.scatter(last_basic.lon, last_basic.lat, color="steelblue",
           s=12, alpha=0.6, label="CMEMS only (day 10)")

# Coupled: prominent
for tid, grp in df_coup.groupby("traj"):
    ax.plot(grp.lon, grp.lat, color="crimson", lw=0.5, alpha=0.10)
last_coup = df_coup.groupby("traj").tail(1)
ax.scatter(last_coup.lon, last_coup.lat, color="crimson",
           s=12, alpha=0.8, label="all forcings + settling (day 10)")

ax.set_xlim(88, 90.5); ax.set_ylim(21, 22.8)
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Effect of full forcing set vs CMEMS-only")
plt.savefig("data/tutorial2_overlay.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
What you should see:

Tides smear the trajectory along an axis. Particles oscillate ±5–10 km tidally over each 12.4-h cycle while drifting with the residual. In a low-frequency plot the coupled cloud will look noisier along the principal tidal axis.
Windage shifts the cloud downwind. January NE monsoon winds push particles toward the SW more strongly than CMEMS alone.
Settling thins the cloud progressively. Particles below ~30 m experience much weaker horizontal drift; the cloud at day 10 is narrower with settling on.

The differences are real but subtle in dry season. Re-run with monsoon-season dates (e.g. --start 2025-08-01 --end 2025-08-15) and the differences become huge.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
section: 18.5 Step 4 — break out each forcing’s contribution
text:
18.5 Step 4 — break out each forcing’s contribution
What if you want to know how much each term contributed? Run five times: baseline, baseline + each one term, full coupled.






Tip



Cache works in your favor. combine_forcings() builds a unique filename for each forcing combination (“__stokes1.0_tides”, “__wind2.0pct”, etc.) and caches the combined NetCDF. The five-runs matrix only re-runs the integrator, not the data combine.


# Currents only (already from Tutorial 1)
# … no extra flags …

# Currents + Stokes
python -m driftscope.simulate ... --stokes data/waves/...waves.nc

# Currents + tides
python -m driftscope.simulate ... --tides data/tides/...tides.nc

# Currents + windage
python -m driftscope.simulate ... \
    --winds data/winds/...winds.nc --windage 0.02

# All four
python -m driftscope.simulate ... --stokes ... --tides ... --winds ...
Then plot the day-10 mean position of each ensemble:
import numpy as np

stems = [
    ("CMEMS only",                  "currents_only"),
    ("+ Stokes",                    "stokes1.0"),
    ("+ tides",                     "tides"),
    ("+ wind 2%",                   "wind2.0pct"),
    ("all forcings",                "stokes1.0_tides_wind2.0pct"),
]

means = []
for label, suffix in stems:
    path = (f"data/trajectories/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29"
            f"__{suffix}_traj.zarr")
    ds = load_trajectories(path)
    df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
    last = df.groupby("traj").tail(1)
    means.append((label,
                  float(last.lon.mean()),
                  float(last.lat.mean())))

for label, x, y in means:
    print(f"{label:25s} → ({x:.4f}°E, {y:.4f}°N)")
You’ll get something like:
CMEMS only                → (88.7821°E, 21.0334°N)
+ Stokes                  → (88.7619°E, 21.0291°N)
+ tides                   → (88.7894°E, 21.0455°N)
+ wind 2%                 → (88.7102°E, 20.9742°N)
all forcings              → (88.6708°E, 20.9588°N)
This is the “term contribution” table. Windage moves the mean by ~7 km in this dry-season setup; Stokes by ~2 km; tides barely shift the mean (they are oscillatory) but spread the cloud.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18.6 What you’ve learned

The coupled simulation is one extra flag per forcing — there is no special API.
The combined-NetCDF cache makes A/B testing efficient.
Tides oscillate, currents and wind drift, settling thins. Each forcing has a distinctive signature you can read off the trajectory cloud.
The dry-season Sundarbans is a mild flow regime; reality gets much more interesting in monsoon and post-cyclone conditions.

title: 17  Tutorial 2 — All forcings together
text:
18.7 What’s still missing
Two big things:

Sub-grid eddies. All five terms above are deterministic. Real ocean trajectories have ~10 km RMS scatter per day from unresolved submesoscale motion. Add --brownian-kh 100 to the simulation; the final cloud broadens by ~20 km after 10 days. The next tutorial (Chapter 19) checks whether 100 m²/s is the right number by comparing against a real GDP drifter.
Reality. All of this is model output. We haven’t compared with a single observation. Tutorial 3 fixes that.

Continue to Chapter 19.

title: 18  Tutorial 3 — Drifter validation
text:
19 Tutorial 3 — Drifter validation
A model is a story until you compare it to data. This tutorial walks through the most informative validation check available for a Lagrangian drift model: simulate a particle from where a real drifter started, overlay the two tracks, compute a skill score.

title: 18  Tutorial 3 — Drifter validation
text:
19.1 The drifter
We use GDP ID 300534064293930 — a NOAA Global Drifter Program drifter that entered the Bay of Bengal from the Andaman Sea in late April 2025 and was tracked for ~6 weeks. Why this drifter:

It’s recent enough that CMEMS and HYCOM both have analyses for it.
Its track crosses the shelf break and a mesoscale eddy in the eastern BoB — exactly the region where 1/12° models historically struggle.
It’s documented in scripts/drifter_validation.py.

title: 18  Tutorial 3 — Drifter validation
text:
19.2 Step 1 — fetch the drifter track
python -m driftscope.drifters \
    --bbox 87,8,95,16 \
    --start 2025-04-20 --end 2025-06-01 \
    --region andaman_to_bob
The fetcher hits NOAA AOML’s ERDDAP server and returns a CSV with hourly positions for any drifter active in the bbox/time window. Output:

title: 18  Tutorial 3 — Drifter validation
text:
19.6 Step 5 — Liu–Weisberg skill score
Distance between the two tracks at each time is a metric, but a single-number summary is more useful. We use Liu–Weisberg skill:
\[
S = 1 - \frac{\sum_n \|\mathbf{X}_\text{sim}(t_n) - \mathbf{X}_\text{real}(t_n)\|}{\sum_n \|\mathbf{X}_\text{real}(t_n) - \mathbf{X}_\text{real}(t_0)\|}
\tag{19.1}\]
Numerator: cumulative displacement error. Denominator: cumulative displacement of the real drifter from its release point (“how far did it go in total”).
Interpretation:

\(S = 1\) — perfect.
\(S = 0\) — model has no skill beyond a stationary particle.
\(S < 0\) — model is worse than predicting “the drifter doesn’t move”.

The +0.15 improvement is real and has a clear physical interpretation: HYCOM’s higher resolution captures the southward eddy that CMEMS smooths over.

19.8 Caveats — what this validation does not show






Warning




Single-drifter case study, not a fleet-wide statistic. A proper validation runs over dozens of drifters with bootstrapped uncertainty. This tutorial does the smallest version.
Drogued drifters track 15-m flow; surface drifters (windage-prone) would score the wind-on configuration differently.
Skill scores are bbox-dependent. A short-range track (drifter released near a coast and recovered after a week) is much easier than a long-range track. Don’t compare LW skills across drifters with different durations.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20 Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
Goal: reproduce the four-panel dynamics figure inspired by Lenain et al. (2026)’s GOFLOW. Walks through what each panel shows, what the resolution limits mean, and how to interpret the result.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.1 What we’re trying to make
Four panels, in a 2×2 grid:

(a) Surface velocity vectors over SST.
(b) \(\log_{10}|\nabla T|\) — the front map.
(c) \(\zeta / f\) — relative vorticity over Coriolis.
(d) \(\delta / f\) — divergence over Coriolis.

The structure is from a GOFLOW figure (Gulf Stream, sub-km resolution GOES-derived currents). We adapt it to HYCOM 1/25° currents + OSTIA L4 SST in the Bay of Bengal.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.2 Step 1 — fetch the data
Pick a wider basin than the Sundarbans default; the snapshot needs open ocean to show eddy structure. We use the GBM pre-monsoon window:
# HYCOM (1/25°) for the open BoB
python -m driftscope.hycom \
    --bbox 87.5,19,92.5,23 \
    --start 2025-04-20 --end 2025-06-01 \
    --region "GBM premonsoon"

# OSTIA SST for the same window
python -m driftscope.sst \
    --bbox 87.5,19,92.5,23 \
    --start 2025-04-20 --end 2025-05-31
(43 days HYCOM ≈ 5 MB; 42 days OSTIA ≈ 700 KB.)

    --time-index 21 \

Flag
Meaning
