title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.4 Step 3 — what the panels mean

20.4.1 Panel (a): velocity over SST
Two fields on one plot. The colormap shows \(T_\text{SST}\) in °C; the arrows show \((u, v)\) vectors at every third grid cell.
Read it as: the SST field is the thermal context. Cold cores = cyclonic eddies (upwelled subsurface water). Warm cores = anticyclonic. Sharp linear boundaries between warm and cold regions are fronts — typically high-shear, biologically productive, and where particle convergence happens.
The velocity vectors should wrap around SST eddies (a cyclonic eddy has counterclockwise flow in the NH) and cross fronts perpendicularly where the flow advects mass through them.






Tip



The inset. A small subplot in the upper right of (a) shows the velocity speed time series at the reference point over the analysis window. Daily-mean HYCOM filters out inertial oscillations (which have ~32 h period at 22°N) — the daily series tells you about synoptic-scale variability (1–2 weeks). For inertial-band signal you’d need hourly currents and a different plot.




20.4.2 Panel (b): log|∇T| — fronts
We compute the magnitude of the SST gradient at every cell:
\[
|\nabla T| = \sqrt{(\partial T/\partial x)^2 + (\partial T/\partial y)^2}
\]
…and plot \(\log_{10}|\nabla T|\) in K/m. Why log: SST gradients span 3+ orders of magnitude (open ocean is smooth; fronts are sharp). Log scaling makes the full range readable in one image.
OSTIA at 5 km resolves a lot of front structure. Open Bay of Bengal during pre-monsoon shows:

Cool SST cap in the NW (mainland river outflows + cooler shelf water).
Warm tongue along the SE Andaman side.
Filaments wrapping eddies at \(|\nabla T| \sim 10^{-4}\) K/m (\(\log = -4\)).

The brightness in panel (b) is the best resolved view of the ocean’s small-scale structure that DriftScope has — even though the velocity model can’t resolve those filaments.


20.4.3 Panel (c): ζ/f — vorticity
From Chapter 7, \(\zeta / f\) measures the local “spin-iness” of the flow relative to background rotation:
\[
\zeta = \partial v / \partial x - \partial u / \partial y, \qquad
f = 2 \Omega \sin\varphi
\]
Plotted on a \(\pm 1\) red-blue colormap: red = positive \(\zeta\) (cyclonic, counterclockwise NH); blue = negative (anticyclonic).
In the wide-bbox snapshot, the dominant feature is a cyclonic eddy near 89.5°E / 22°N with \(\zeta/f \approx +0.5\) at its core. This is the same eddy visible as a cool patch in panel (a) and a wrap of \(|\nabla T|\) filaments in panel (b). When all four panels show the same feature in different ways, you’re looking at a real eddy.


20.4.4 Panel (d): δ/f — divergence
\[
\delta = \partial u / \partial x + \partial v / \partial y
\]
Where \(\delta > 0\), water is diverging — flow exits the cell faster than it enters. By mass conservation, this requires upwelling (water coming from below to fill the surface deficit). \(\delta < 0\) implies convergence and downwelling.
Divergence is much smaller than vorticity in geostrophic flow (where incompressibility forces \(\delta \approx 0\)). Non-geostrophic features (fronts, filaments, ageostrophic eddies) light up here.
DriftScope’s HYCOM at 4 km strains hardest in this panel: \(\delta/f\) ranges \(\pm 0.2\), much noisier-looking than the cleaner \(\zeta/f\) field. This is the model’s resolution edge — what’s signal and what’s discretization noise gets harder to tell.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.5 Step 4 — resolution caveat






Warning



The figure inspired this book because it shows something the model doesn’t see. The original GOFLOW panels show submesoscale filaments at sub-kilometer resolution. HYCOM at 4 km gives a macro version — the same eddies, smoothed. OSTIA SST at 5 km gives sharp fronts; HYCOM velocities at 4 km give blurry vorticity.
This mismatch is itself a useful figure. Side-by-side, panels (b) and (c) tell you “the ocean is sharper than the velocity model thinks”. For the full GOFLOW-style sub-km picture in the BoB, you’d need either a regional ROMS/CROCO run or future SWOT/GOFLOW-style products that cover that region.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.6 Step 5 — variations
A few useful variants:
# Different day in the window
python scripts/sundarban_dynamics_snapshot.py \
    --time-index 5      # day 5 — earlier in pre-monsoon

# Smaller bbox (Sundarbans)
python scripts/sundarban_dynamics_snapshot.py \
    --currents data/currents/sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01_hycom.nc \
    --sst data/sst/sundarbans_delta_2026-04-17_2026-05-01_sst.nc \
    --time-index 7

# Animate over the full window
for i in $(seq 0 42); do
    python scripts/sundarban_dynamics_snapshot.py \
        --time-index $i \
        --out data/dynamics_$(printf '%03d' $i).png
done
ffmpeg -framerate 4 -i data/dynamics_%03d.png \
    -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p data/dynamics_animation.mp4
The animation makes the eddy life cycle visible: spin-up, mature, detach, dissipate. Static snapshots miss the time evolution.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.7 Step 6 — in the bigger picture
This figure is not a particle simulation. It’s an Eulerian diagnostic of the velocity field that drives the simulation. You’d make one of these for every region/season you simulate, before running the trajectory model — to know what features the model resolves (visible eddies in \(\zeta/f\)) and what it doesn’t (sharp fronts in \(|\nabla T|\) that don’t show up in \(\zeta/f\)).
In a paper or report:

“We simulated 10-day drift with DriftScope. The dominant velocity feature in the simulation period was a cyclonic eddy at ~89°E (panel c, \(\zeta/f \approx 0.5\)) co-located with a 1°C cool SST anomaly (panel a). Particles released within the eddy rotated 1.5 cycles before exiting; particles outside drifted SW under the residual monsoon flow.”

That paragraph is impossible to write without the dynamics snapshot. With it, the simulation has physical context.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.8 Reusable diagnostics
The math used in the script — gradient → curl/divergence → normalize by Coriolis — is also exposed as a single helper in driftscope/diagnostics.py:22:
from driftscope.diagnostics import compute_diagnostics, plot_diagnostics

d = compute_diagnostics(u, v, lats, lons)
print(d.keys())  # dict_keys(['speed', 'vorticity', 'divergence',
                 #            'grad_mag', 'rossby_vort', 'rossby_div', 'f'])
fig = plot_diagnostics(u, v, lats, lons, time_str="2025-05-10")
Use the helpers when you want the diagnostic fields for further analysis (FFTs, ensemble statistics). Use the script when you want the panel figure.

title: 19  Tutorial 4 — The dynamics snapshot
text:
20.9 Summary

Four panels reveal complementary aspects of the surface flow: vectors over SST, fronts, vorticity, divergence.
Computed at the model’s native grid with simple finite differences and the Coriolis parameter at the local latitude.
Resolution-limited: 4 km HYCOM cannot resolve the submesoscale filaments visible in 5 km OSTIA SST. The mismatch is informative.
One command produces it; reusable helpers in diagnostics.py for custom analyses.

The final tutorial puts it all together — a seasonal-comparison run that exercises every module in this book.




Lenain, L. et al. (2026). GOFLOW: Geostationary ocean flow. Nature Geoscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-01943-0

title: 20  Tutorial 5 — Seasonal dispersion
text:
21 Tutorial 5 — Seasonal dispersion
The Bay of Bengal has a bimodal monsoon flow regime: sluggish northeast-flowing residual in the dry season (Jan–Feb), strong southwest-flowing monsoon current in summer (Jul–Aug), with shoulder seasons of pre- and post-monsoon. The dispersion of a sediment release looks completely different in each season — same release point, different ocean.
This tutorial builds the four-season comparison: 2×2 mosaic + per-season animations. It exercises every module in the book.

21.1 What the goal looks like

title: 20  Tutorial 5 — Seasonal dispersion
text:
21.2 The architecture
The seasonal-comparison pipeline has three steps:

For each season, fetch all forcings (currents, waves, winds, tides), the SPM map (one representative dry-season Sentinel-2 scene reused as a release pattern), and run a coupled simulation.
For each season, render a single PNG/GIF showing the dispersion.
Combine the four into a single 2×2 mosaic and a comparison GIF.

scripts/run_seasonal_dispersion.py does step 1; scripts/build_seasonal_comparison.py does steps 2 and 3.

21.3 Step 1 — fetch all forcings, all seasons
For each season, the four forcings:
SEASONS=(
    "dry         2025-01-15 2025-02-14"
    "premonsoon  2025-04-20 2025-06-01"
    "monsoon     2025-08-01 2025-08-31"
    "postmonsoon 2025-10-15 2025-11-14"
)

for s in "${SEASONS[@]}"; do
    read name start end <<< "$s"
    region="gbm_$name"
    bbox="87.5,19,92.5,23"

    python -m driftscope.hycom    --bbox $bbox --start $start --end $end --region "$region"
    python -m driftscope.stokes   --bbox $bbox --start $start --end $end --region "$region"
    python -m driftscope.tides    --bbox $bbox --start $start --end $end --region "$region"
    python -m driftscope.winds    --bbox $bbox --start $start --end $end --region "$region"
done

Why HYCOM, not CMEMS, for seasonal? The dispersion patterns are visibly different between the two products. HYCOM’s higher resolution captures the EICC narrowing in pre-monsoon and the eddy shedding off the southern Bangladesh shelf in monsoon. CMEMS smooths these. For a seasonal-comparison figure, HYCOM is the better story.

title: 20  Tutorial 5 — Seasonal dispersion
text:
21.6 What you should see
Each panel shows particle positions over time:

Dry: small cloud, ~30 km/day to the SW. Weak signal.
Pre-monsoon: cloud elongates SE under the building East India Coastal Current. Faster.
Monsoon: cloud accelerates south, picks up the strong wind-driven Ekman + windage. Reaches ~150 km away in 30 days; a long thin streak.
Post-monsoon: cloud reverses direction (EICC flips north), returns part-way. Sometimes loops back near the release point.







Tip



The post-monsoon reversal is the most counterintuitive result of the project. Sediment released in the same place can end up in opposite parts of the basin depending on which season you look at. This is the kind of insight only a Lagrangian model can give you — an Eulerian plot of the residual current at one moment doesn’t tell you “where will the stuff go” because the answer depends on when the stuff was released.

title: 20  Tutorial 5 — Seasonal dispersion
text:
21.7 Step 4 — quantify, don’t just plot
A pretty 2×2 isn’t science by itself. Two quantitative summaries:

21.7.1 4a — dispersion ellipse per season
Fit a 2D Gaussian to the final particle positions:
import numpy as np
from driftscope.viz import load_trajectories, traj_to_dataframe

seasons = ["dry", "premonsoon", "monsoon", "postmonsoon"]
results = {}

for s in seasons:
    ds = load_trajectories(
        f"data/trajectories/coupled_spm_hycom_brownian_{s}_30d.zarr"
    )
    df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
    last = df.groupby("traj").tail(1)

    cov = np.cov(last.lon, last.lat)
    eig, vec = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
    major = np.sqrt(eig[1]) * 111   # convert deg to km approximately
    minor = np.sqrt(eig[0]) * 111
    angle = np.degrees(np.arctan2(vec[1, 1], vec[0, 1]))
    centroid = (last.lon.mean(), last.lat.mean())

    results[s] = {
        "centroid": centroid,
        "major_km": major, "minor_km": minor,
        "angle_deg": angle,
    }

for s, r in results.items():
    print(f"{s:12s}  centroid {r['centroid'][0]:.3f}°E, "
          f"{r['centroid'][1]:.3f}°N | "
          f"major axis {r['major_km']:5.1f} km @ {r['angle_deg']:+5.0f}°")
Typical output (varies with seed):
dry           centroid 89.150°E, 21.040°N | major axis  78.0 km @ +35°
premonsoon    centroid 89.460°E, 20.530°N | major axis  95.0 km @ +20°
monsoon       centroid 89.730°E, 20.160°N | major axis 145.0 km @ +12°
postmonsoon   centroid 89.080°E, 21.500°N | major axis 102.0 km @ +60°
The numbers tell the same story as the GIF: monsoon disperses much farther; post-monsoon angle changes; centroid migrates seasonally.


21.7.2 4b — fraction reaching the open ocean
Define “open ocean” as bbox south of 20°N (offshore of the BoB shelf). Compute the fraction of particles that crossed it in each season:
for s in seasons:
    ds = load_trajectories(
        f"data/trajectories/coupled_spm_hycom_brownian_{s}_30d.zarr"
    )
    df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
    last = df.groupby("traj").tail(1)
    pct = 100 * (last.lat < 20).mean()
    print(f"{s:12s}  → open ocean: {pct:.0f}%")
dry           → open ocean: 8%

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22 Adding a new region
DriftScope is region-agnostic: the bbox is a parameter, not a constant. But adding a named region (so it shows up in the CLI choices and in PRESETS) is a one-file change. This chapter walks through it for a new delta — say the Mahanadi in eastern India.

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.1 The pattern
A region is just a Region dataclass entry in driftscope/config.py’s PRESETS dict. Existing entries:
PRESETS: dict[str, Region] = {
    "sundarbans": Region(
        "Sundarbans Delta", 88.0, 90.5, 21.0, 22.8,
        seed_lon=89.0, seed_lat=21.2,
    ),
    "northern_bay_of_bengal": Region(
        "Northern Bay of Bengal", 86.5, 92.5, 19.5, 23.0,
        seed_lon=89.5, seed_lat=20.5,
    ),
    "bay_of_bengal": Region("Bay of Bengal (broad)", 80.0, 95.0, 10.0, 23.0),
    "hooghly_mouth": Region(
        "Hooghly River Mouth", 87.8, 89.0, 21.2, 22.2,
        seed_lon=88.6, seed_lat=21.4,
    ),
    "gulf_stream": Region("Gulf Stream", -75.0, -60.0, 35.0, 44.0),
    "california": Region("California Current", -127.0, -117.0, 32.0, 42.0),
}
Each entry has:








Field
Required
Purpose




name
yes
Pretty label used in plot titles and filenames


lon_min, lat_min, lon_max, lat_max
yes
Bbox corners


seed_lon, seed_lat
optional
Default release point if bbox center is on land

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.2 Step 1 — pick the bbox
For Mahanadi, the river mouth is at ~86.7°E, 20.3°N. The shelf extends ~50 km offshore. A useful bbox spans a wide enough area for a 30-day particle plume to stay inside.
Rule of thumb: bbox size \(\geq\) peak speed × runtime × 1.5 in each direction. Bay of Bengal monsoon current ≈ 0.5 m/s × 30 days × 86400 = 1300 km. So at 20°N, ~12° in lon and lat. That’s basin-scale; for a local-shelf study a smaller bbox is fine because particles will leave it and DeleteOOB handles them.
For a local Mahanadi study:
"mahanadi": Region(
    "Mahanadi Delta", 86.0, 88.5, 19.5, 21.0,
    seed_lon=86.7, seed_lat=20.2,
),

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.3 Step 2 — add the entry
Edit driftscope/config.py:
PRESETS: dict[str, Region] = {
    # ... existing entries ...
    "mahanadi": Region(
        "Mahanadi Delta", 86.0, 88.5, 19.5, 21.0,
        seed_lon=86.7, seed_lat=20.2,
    ),
    # ... rest of dict ...
}
That’s it. The new region is now available as a CLI choice in every fetcher and the simulator:
python -m driftscope.fetch  --region mahanadi
python -m driftscope.simulate --region mahanadi

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.4 Step 3 — fetch and run
# Currents (CMEMS or HYCOM)
python -m driftscope.fetch --region mahanadi --days 14
python -m driftscope.hycom --region mahanadi --start 2025-08-01 --end 2025-08-15

# Optional forcings
python -m driftscope.stokes --region mahanadi --days 14
python -m driftscope.winds  --region mahanadi --days 14
python -m driftscope.tides  --region mahanadi --days 14

# Run a basic simulation
python -m driftscope.simulate --region mahanadi --days 10
All cached as mahanadi_delta_<dates>_<kind>.{nc,csv} — no overwrite of existing Sundarbans data.

title: 21  Adding a new region
section: 22.5 Step 4 — check the bbox isn’t broken
text:
22.5 Step 4 — check the bbox isn’t broken
A few things can go subtly wrong with a new region:






Warning



Mostly land. If the bbox is mostly land, particles can’t be seeded. Inspect the currents file:
import xarray as xr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ds = xr.open_dataset("data/currents/mahanadi_delta_<dates>.nc")
ds.uo.isel(time=0).plot()
plt.savefig("mahanadi_check.png")
The white pixels are land. If the bbox is >70% white, your seed disk needs to be offshore of the bbox center. Set seed_lon, seed_lat accordingly.








Warning



Bbox crosses the antimeridian (Pacific). HYCOM uses 0..360 longitude; CMEMS uses -180..180. The fetchers handle one wrap each but not bboxes that cross 0/360 (lon -178 to +178). Pick a bbox that stays on one side. Look at driftscope/hycom.py:71 for the explicit NotImplementedError.








Warning



Equatorial regions. \(f \to 0\) at the equator, so \(\zeta/f\) and \(\delta/f\) in the dynamics snapshot blow up. The diagnostics module masks this with f_safe = np.where(np.abs(f) < 1e-10, np.nan, f). For a region that includes the equator (e.g. Indonesian throughflow), the dynamics figure shows NaN there — correct, not a bug.

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.6 Step 5 — region-specific tuning
Different regions warrant different defaults. A few knobs to consider adjusting:

Brownian \(K_h\): 100 m²/s is BoB-tuned. Ekman-current-dominated regions (Pacific equatorial) need lower; eddy-rich regions (Kuroshio, Gulf Stream) need higher. Validate against drifters.
Settling diameter: 10 µm is silt for the BoB. Flocculated organic muds (e.g. Mississippi delta) settle slower; coarser shelf sands settle faster. Tune to your sediment.
Windage coefficient: 2% is sediment-laden water. Plastic debris is 3%; oil slicks 3.5%. Match to your tracer.
Tide model: TPXO9-atlas-v5 has good local refinement near major coastlines. For polar regions or Arctic shelves, FES2014 or the AOTIM regional models are better. Change TIDE_MODEL_NAME in config.py:139.

These are per-run parameters, not per-region — but a wrapper script that sets sensible defaults for each named region is a useful pattern. See scripts/run_seasonal_dispersion.py:36–49 for the BoB defaults bundled into one script.

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.7 Step 6 — share the work
Once a new region is working:

Validate with at least one GDP drifter (Chapter 19).
Document the choice of defaults — Brownian \(K_h\), settling diameter, etc. — in a memory file or comment.
Commit the config.py entry along with a short script that exercises it. Future-you (or your student) will need to find the “happy path” for the new region.

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.8 Other “regions” — non-geographic
The pattern works for non-geographic modes too. For example:

gulf_stream in the existing presets is a non-Sundarbans region used for testing CMEMS and HYCOM behavior in a known-energetic environment.
A test preset with a tiny bbox could be added for unit tests that need real data without a 5-minute download.

The point is: PRESETS is a registry of named experiments. Use it for whatever named experiment makes sense.

title: 21  Adding a new region
text:
22.9 Summary

A new region is one entry in PRESETS.
Once added, it works in every fetcher and the simulator.
Watch for mostly-land bboxes, antimeridian crossings, and equatorial Coriolis singularities — three documented gotchas.
Region-specific physics defaults (Brownian, settling) belong in a per-region wrapper script, not in config.py.

Next: how to add a new forcing, which is a bigger lift than a new region but still a fixed pattern.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23 Adding a new forcing
Most extensions to DriftScope are new terms in the master equation Eq. 5.2. This chapter walks through the end-to-end pattern for adding one, using a hypothetical internal-wave drift module as the worked example. By the end you’ll know which files to touch, which to leave alone, and how to verify the new term actually does something.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23.1 The four pieces
Every velocity-field forcing in DriftScope has the same four pieces:

A fetcher — driftscope/<name>.py that downloads or computes the data and saves it as a NetCDF with (time, latitude, longitude) coordinates and named velocity components.
A combine_forcings() clause — driftscope/simulate.py:47 adds the new field to the existing currents.
A SimConfig flag — driftscope/config.py’s SimConfig dataclass adds an include_<name> boolean and any tuning parameters.
A CLI flag — driftscope/simulate.py’s main() adds --<name> and --<param> arguments.

For a per-particle forcing (settling, Brownian) the pattern is slightly different — see Section 23.3 below.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23.2 Worked example: internal-wave drift
Internal waves at the pycnocline produce a small Stokes-drift-analog mean flow at the surface. Let’s add it.

23.2.1 Piece 1 — the fetcher
Create driftscope/internal_waves.py:
"""Internal-wave-induced surface drift.

Internal waves at the pycnocline shed surface trapped energy into a
weak (~1-2 cm/s) mean drift via wave–wave nonlinear interactions. Less
well-quantified than Stokes drift; we use a simple parameterization
based on the local mixed-layer depth and surface stratification.

Currently: a placeholder that computes uniform 1 cm/s eastward drift —
useful as a unit test for the new-forcing extension pattern.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr
from rich.console import Console

from .config import IW_DIR  # add this to config.py

console = Console()


def output_path(region_name: str, start: str, end: str) -> Path:
    safe = region_name.lower().replace(" ", "_")
    return IW_DIR / f"{safe}_{start}_{end}_iw.nc"


def fetch_iw_drift(bbox, start_date, end_date,
                   currents_nc, region_name="custom", force=False):
    """Compute a placeholder uniform 1 cm/s eastward IW drift.

    For a real implementation, replace the body with a model query
    (e.g. Whalen et al. 2020 climatology) or a derivation from
    CMEMS T/S profiles.
    """
    out = output_path(region_name, start_date, end_date)
    if out.exists() and not force:
        console.print(f"[green]✓[/green] cached: {out.name}")
        return out

    cur = xr.open_dataset(currents_nc)
    lon_name = "longitude" if "longitude" in cur.coords else "lon"
    lat_name = "latitude" if "latitude" in cur.coords else "lat"

    # Match the currents grid for spatial coordinates; daily for time.
    times = cur["time"].values
    lons = cur[lon_name].values
    lats = cur[lat_name].values

    u_iw = np.full((len(times), len(lats), len(lons)), 0.01, dtype="float32")
    v_iw = np.zeros_like(u_iw)

    ds = xr.Dataset(
        data_vars={
            "u_iw": (("time", lat_name, lon_name), u_iw,
                     {"long_name": "Internal-wave drift, eastward",
                      "units": "m s-1"}),
            "v_iw": (("time", lat_name, lon_name), v_iw,
                     {"long_name": "Internal-wave drift, northward",
                      "units": "m s-1"}),
        },
        coords={"time": times, lat_name: lats, lon_name: lons},
    )
    ds.to_netcdf(out)
    console.print(f"[green]✓[/green] saved {out.name}")
    return out


def main():
    import argparse
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Compute IW-drift placeholder")
    p.add_argument("--bbox", required=True, type=str)
    p.add_argument("--start", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--end", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--region", default="custom")
    p.add_argument("--currents", required=True, type=Path)
    p.add_argument("--force", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    bbox = tuple(float(x) for x in args.bbox.split(","))
    fetch_iw_drift(bbox, args.start, args.end, args.currents,
                   args.region, args.force)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


23.2.2 Piece 2 — extend combine_forcings()
In driftscope/simulate.py:47, add the new clause to combine_forcings():
def combine_forcings(
    currents_nc, stokes_nc=None, tides_nc=None, winds_nc=None,
    iw_nc=None,                # NEW
    stokes_scale=1.0, windage_coeff=0.03,
):
    tag = []
    if stokes_nc:  tag.append(f"stokes{stokes_scale:.1f}")
    if tides_nc:   tag.append("tides")
    if winds_nc:   tag.append(f"wind{windage_coeff*100:.1f}pct")
    if iw_nc:      tag.append("iw")        # NEW
    suffix = ("__" + "_".join(tag)) if tag else "__currents_only"
    out = currents_nc.with_name(f"{currents_nc.stem}{suffix}.nc")

    inputs = [currents_nc] + [p for p in (stokes_nc, tides_nc, winds_nc, iw_nc)
                               if p is not None]
    # ... existing time-grid logic ...

    if iw_nc is not None:                  # NEW BLOCK
        iw = xr.open_dataset(iw_nc)
        iw_lon = "longitude" if "longitude" in iw.coords else "lon"
        iw_lat = "latitude" if "latitude" in iw.coords else "lat"
        u_iw = iw["u_iw"].interp(
            {iw_lon: cur[cur_lon], iw_lat: cur[cur_lat], "time": time_grid},
        ).fillna(0.0)
        v_iw = iw["v_iw"].interp(
            {iw_lon: cur[cur_lon], iw_lat: cur[cur_lat], "time": time_grid},
        ).fillna(0.0)
        uo = uo + u_iw
        vo = vo + v_iw

    combined = cur_resampled.copy()
    combined["uo"] = uo; combined["vo"] = vo
    combined.to_netcdf(out)
    return out
The pattern is identical to the existing Stokes/tides/winds blocks: open the file, interpolate to the currents grid+time, fill NaN with 0, add to uo/vo.


23.2.3 Piece 3 — SimConfig and call sites
In driftscope/config.py, extend SimConfig:
@dataclass
class SimConfig:
    # ... existing fields ...
    include_iw: bool = False    # NEW

    # path constant near the top of config.py
    IW_DIR = DATA / "internal_waves"
And in driftscope/simulate.py:165, run_simulation()’s signature gains iw_nc: Path | None = None. The “active forcings” log line and the combine_forcings() call gain the IW path:
def run_simulation(currents_nc, cfg, ..., iw_nc=None):
    use_iw = cfg.include_iw and iw_nc is not None
    if use_stokes or use_tides or use_winds or use_iw:    # NEW
        active = [...]
        if use_iw: active.append("IW")                    # NEW
        ...
        currents_nc = combine_forcings(
            currents_nc,
            stokes_nc=...,
            tides_nc=...,
            winds_nc=...,
            iw_nc=iw_nc if use_iw else None,              # NEW
        )


23.2.4 Piece 4 — CLI flag
In driftscope/simulate.py’s main():
p.add_argument("--iw", type=Path, default=None,
               help="internal-wave drift NetCDF "
                    "(from `python -m driftscope.internal_waves`)")
# ...
cfg = SimConfig(
    # ...
    include_iw=args.iw is not None,
)
run_simulation(
    currents, cfg,
    stokes_nc=args.stokes, tides_nc=args.tides,
    winds_nc=args.winds, iw_nc=args.iw,        # NEW
)
That’s it. ~80 lines across three files for a complete new forcing.


23.2.5 How to verify it works
# 1) Fetch the new field
python -m driftscope.internal_waves \
    --bbox 88,21,90.5,22.8 --start 2025-01-15 --end 2025-01-29 \
    --region sundarbans \
    --currents data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc

# 2) Run a baseline + IW simulation
python -m driftscope.simulate \
    --currents data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc

python -m driftscope.simulate \
    --currents data/currents/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29.nc \
    --iw data/internal_waves/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29_iw.nc

# 3) Compare day-10 mean positions
python -c "
from driftscope.viz import load_trajectories, traj_to_dataframe
for suffix in ['currents_only', 'iw']:
    ds = load_trajectories(f'data/trajectories/sundarbans_2025-01-15_2025-01-29__{suffix}_traj.zarr')
    df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
    last = df.groupby('traj').tail(1)
    print(f'{suffix:15s}  mean ({last.lon.mean():.4f}E, {last.lat.mean():.4f}N)')
"
With a uniform 1 cm/s eastward drift over 10 days, particles should shift ~8.6 km east of the no-IW case. Verify the longitude differs by ~0.08° (\(\approx 8.6\) km / 111 km/°).
If yes: end-to-end pattern works. Replace the placeholder content in internal_waves.py with real physics.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23.3 Per-particle forcings — kernels
A per-particle forcing — different velocities for different particles at the same location — needs a kernel, not a field. Examples:

Settling (different sizes → different vertical velocities).
Reaction kinetics (a particle decays over time).
Buoyancy depending on a per-particle density attribute.

The pattern is similar but lives in driftscope/kernels.py:
def MyPerParticleKernel(particle, fieldset, time):
    # update particle.lon, particle.lat, particle.depth, or any per-particle
    # variable using `particle_dlon`/`particle_dlat`/`particle_ddepth`.
    pass
…and driftscope/simulate.py:380 (kernel chain assembly):
kernels = [AdvectionRK4]
if use_settling: kernels.append(Settling)
if use_brownian: kernels.append(BrownianMotion2D)
if use_my_kernel: kernels.append(MyPerParticleKernel)   # NEW
kernels.append(DeleteOOB)
If your kernel needs per-particle attributes, define a custom particle class (see SedimentParticle at simulate.py:235 for an example) and pass it to ParticleSet.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23.4 Pitfalls






Warning



Time-grid mismatch. Different forcings live on different time grids (daily currents, 6-hourly winds, hourly tides). combine_forcings() already handles this: it picks the finest time grid present and interpolates. Just make sure your fetcher writes a time coordinate that is at least as fine as currents, and combine_forcings will align it.








Warning



Unit consistency. All forcings must produce m/s velocity. If your data source uses cm/s, mm/day, or knots, convert in the fetcher before saving. Past gotcha: pyTMD returns cm/s; tides.py multiplies by 0.01 to get m/s.








Warning



Cache filename collision. The cache filename incorporates all active forcings — __stokes1.0_tides_wind2.0pct_iw.nc. If you forget to add your tag in combine_forcings()’s tag list, two runs with and without your forcing will overwrite the same combined-NetCDF cache and silently produce wrong simulations. Always add the tag.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23.5 Validation
A new forcing is not done until you’ve shown it changes a meaningful answer. Minimum bar:

Smoke test: simulation runs end to end, doesn’t crash.
Quantitative test: with the forcing on vs off, the day-10 particle cloud’s mean position differs by an amount you can predict from the magnitude of your new term.
Drifter test: re-run the validation tutorial; does the LW skill score change in the right direction? If yes, you’re adding signal. If no, you’re adding noise.
Edge case: what happens at the equator? At the antimeridian? In regions with land coverage > 50%?

Each is fast. Skip them and your forcing module will haunt the codebase.

title: 22  Adding a new forcing
text:
23.6 Summary

New forcings follow a fixed four-piece pattern: fetcher, combine clause, SimConfig flag, CLI flag.
The pattern is uniform across Stokes, tides, winds — adding the fifth field uses the same shape as the first.
Per-particle physics goes in kernels.py, not in fields. Different pattern, but simpler.
Validate: smoke test, quantitative test, drifter test, edge case.

This closes the Extending part. The appendices cover the glossary and the three failure modes new students hit most often.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Glossary
Terms a student new to physical oceanography meets in this book. In roughly the order they appear, with the chapter that defines them.
Advection — transport of a quantity (mass, heat, particles) by the bulk motion of a fluid. The dominant transport mechanism for surface material. Chapter 6
Barotropic — depending only on pressure (not on density structure). Tidal currents are barotropic to good approximation: \(u_\text{tide}\) is nearly the same at the surface and 50 m down. Chapter 13
Brownian motion — random walk parameterizing unresolved sub-grid eddy variability. Gaussian increments per timestep, scaled by the horizontal diffusivity \(K_h\). Chapter 10
Cluster-based regression (CBR) — algorithm for retrieving water properties (SPM, depth, chlorophyll) from multispectral imagery in optically heterogeneous regions. Partitions the spectrum into classes first, fits a regression per class. Chapter 15
Coriolis parameter \(f\) — half the projection of Earth’s angular velocity onto the local vertical. \(f = 2\Omega \sin\varphi\). Drives the inertial oscillation. Chapter 7
Dispersion (Lagrangian) — spread of a particle ensemble due to the shear of the mean flow. Distinct from diffusion. Dominates over diffusion at scales > ~10 km in the Bay of Bengal. Chapter 10
Diffusion — spread of a particle ensemble due to random (typically Gaussian) increments. In DriftScope, parameterized by Brownian motion with diffusivity \(K_h\). Chapter 10
Divergence \(\delta\) — \(\delta = \partial u/\partial x + \partial
v/\partial y\). Where \(\delta > 0\), water is leaving the cell (upwelling implied). Geostrophic flow has \(\delta = 0\); ageostrophic features have \(\delta \neq 0\). Chapter 7
East India Coastal Current (EICC) — the seasonally-reversing boundary current along the east coast of India. NE-flowing in winter/spring, SW-flowing in summer monsoon. The dominant deterministic flow in the western Bay of Bengal. Chapter 21
Ekman current — wind-driven current that spirals with depth in the Northern Hemisphere (clockwise from the surface). Important contribution to the surface flow that CMEMS represents in \(\mathbf{u}_\text{currents}\).
Eulerian — describing a fluid by its velocity field \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}, t)\) at fixed locations. The frame of reference of CMEMS, HYCOM, and most ocean datasets. Chapter 5
Floc — porous aggregate of clay-size particles bound by organic and electrostatic forces. Ubiquitous in estuarine SPM; effective settling velocity is much smaller than that of an individual constituent grain. Chapter 9
Geostrophic balance — the balance between the Coriolis force and the horizontal pressure gradient. Dominant balance for large-scale mid-latitude flow. Implies \(\delta \approx 0\) to leading order.
GOFLOW — Geostationary Ocean Flow. The Lenain et al. 2026 method for deriving sub-km surface currents from GOES-East SST. The four-panel figure that motivates Chapter 20 is from this paper.
Inertial period \(T_i = 2\pi / |f|\) — the period of free oscillation of a fluid parcel under Coriolis alone. ~32 h at the Sundarbans (22°N). Chapter 7
Lagrangian — describing a fluid by trajectories of individual parcels: \(\mathbf{X}(t)\) from \(\mathbf{X}(t_0)\). The frame of reference of drifters and DriftScope simulations. Chapter 5
Liu–Weisberg skill score (LW) — normalized error metric for a simulated trajectory vs an observed one. \(S = 1\) perfect; \(S = 0\) no better than a stationary particle. Chapter 19
M2 — the principal lunar semidiurnal tide. Period 12.42 h. The largest harmonic constituent in most of the world ocean.
Mesoscale — ocean variability at scales 10–500 km, periods days to months. Eddies, fronts. CMEMS at 1/12° resolves it; submesoscale features escape it.
Multispectral — referring to imagery sampled in a few discrete spectral bands (e.g. Sentinel-2’s 13 bands). Distinguished from hyperspectral (hundreds of contiguous bands) and panchromatic (one broadband). Chapter 15
OceanParcels — open-source Lagrangian framework that DriftScope builds on. Provides JIT-compiled particle integration, the FieldSet abstraction, and the kernel chain.
Optimal interpolation (OI) — gap-filling and merging algorithm used by L4 SST products (OSTIA) to combine multiple sensors into one gap-free field. Chapter 14
ORCA — the curvilinear (tripolar) grid the NEMO model uses. CMEMS GLORYS products are on ORCA grids; bbox-subset queries hide this from us by interpolating to a regular lon/lat output.
Parcels — see OceanParcels.
Reanalysis — a model run forced and constrained by past data (observations are assimilated). ERA5 is the canonical atmospheric reanalysis; CMEMS GLORYS is the ocean equivalent.
Rossby number — dimensionless measure of how strongly the flow deviates from geostrophic balance. \(Ro = U / fL\). In DriftScope’s diagnostics, \(\zeta/f\) and \(\delta/f\) are local Rossby numbers. Chapter 7
RK4 — Runge–Kutta 4. The fourth-order explicit time integrator. Four velocity probes per step, error scales as \(\Delta t^4\). Chapter 6
Settling velocity \(w_s\) — the terminal vertical velocity of a sinking particle. For small spheres in laminar flow, given by Stokes’ law. Chapter 9
Significant wave height \(H_s\) — the average height of the highest 1/3 of waves in a sea state. The conventional summary of wave amplitude in oceanography. Chapter 8
SPM — Suspended Particulate Matter, in mg/L. The concentration of sediment and other particulates in the water column. The target quantity in Chapter 15.
Stokes drift — wave-induced second-order mean flow. Particles under deep-water waves drift slowly in the direction of wave propagation; a known closed-form approximation gives \(U_s\) from \(H_s\), \(T_m\). Chapter 8
Stokes’ law (settling) — \(w_s = (\rho_p - \rho_w)gd^2/(18\mu)\). Valid for particle Reynolds < 0.5. Chapter 9
Submesoscale — ocean variability at 0.1–10 km, hours to days. Filaments, fronts, ageostrophic eddies. Below CMEMS’ and HYCOM’s resolution; visible in OSTIA SST gradients and in GOFLOW-derived currents.
TPXO9 — Topex/Poseidon-derived tide model from Oregon State. Global, 13 constituents, 1/6° base + 1/30° local refinements. The tide model DriftScope defaults to. Chapter 13
Trajectory — the path of a Lagrangian particle through space-time: \(\mathbf{X}(t)\). The output of a DriftScope simulation. Chapter 5
Vorticity \(\zeta\) — vertical component of the curl of the horizontal velocity. \(\zeta = \partial v/\partial x - \partial u/\partial y\). Positive = cyclonic (counterclockwise NH). Chapter 7
Windage — direct wind drag on the air-exposed fraction of a floating object. \(\mathbf{u}_\text{windage} = \alpha \mathbf{u}_{10}\) with \(\alpha\) small (1–4%). Chapter 8
Zarr — chunked binary storage format used by DriftScope for trajectory output. Reads natively into xarray; supports parallel I/O and cloud-friendly access patterns.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
Troubleshooting
A field guide to the failure modes a new student is likely to hit. Organized by symptom; each entry has the root cause and the fix.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.1 Setup

B.1.1 conda env create errors out on parcels
Symptom: ResolvePackageNotFound: parcels=3.x or compiler errors during the build of parcels.
Root cause: parcels has C extensions that need a working compiler. On macOS, this means Xcode CLI tools; on Linux, gcc.
Fix: install build tools. On macOS: xcode-select --install. On Ubuntu: sudo apt-get install build-essential. Then retry conda env create -f environment.yml.
If still failing, try mamba (conda install -n base mamba; mamba env create -f environment.yml) — mamba’s solver is faster and more reliable.


B.1.2 cartopy import error about GEOS or PROJ
Symptom: OSError: Could not find/load shared object file: libgeos_c.so.1
Root cause: cartopy’s binary doesn’t match the conda-installed geos/proj versions.
Fix:
conda update -n driftscope cartopy proj geos
Or, more aggressive: conda remove cartopy && conda install -c conda-forge cartopy.


B.1.3 python -m driftscope.fetch opens a browser asking for login
Symptom: copernicusmarine.subset() halts and tries to open a browser window for OAuth login.
Root cause: COPERNICUSMARINE_USERNAME / _PASSWORD not in env.
Fix: edit .env, fill in your credentials. Run from the repo root so load_dotenv() finds it. Sanity check:
python -c "import os; print(os.environ.get('COPERNICUSMARINE_USERNAME'))"

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.2 Data fetch

B.2.1 CDS request hangs forever
Symptom: cds.retrieve(...) for ERA5 sits at “Queued” or “Running” for >5 minutes.
Root cause: Big requests on busy days take a while. Most BoB requests finish in 30–90 seconds.
Fix: be patient. If you’re really stuck, log into cds.climate.copernicus.eu and check your queue — sometimes the API key is rate-limited and the request didn’t even submit.


B.2.2 HYCOM fetch fails with HTTP 503 / 404
Symptom: HTTPError: 503 Service Unavailable from tds.hycom.org.
Root cause: The HYCOM THREDDS server has weekly maintenance windows (typically Thursdays 18:00 UTC) when OPeNDAP requests fail.
Fix: wait a few hours and retry. If persistent, switch to CMEMS for the day’s work — the rest of the pipeline is unchanged.


B.2.3 Drifter fetch returns empty CSV
Symptom: data/drifters/<region>_<dates>_drifters.csv has 4 lines (header + units + 0 rows).
Root cause: No GDP drifter active in the bbox/time. This is normal — drifters are sparse.
Fix: widen the bbox or shift the dates. The eastern BoB has the densest drifter coverage in the region; try (85, 8, 95, 16) for 2025-04 onward.


B.2.4 TPXO tide fetch errors with “TIDE_MODEL_DIR not set”
Symptom: RuntimeError: TIDE_MODEL_DIR not set in .env.
Root cause: Tides require a manual one-time setup (TPXO download).
Fix: register at tpxo.net, download TPXO9-atlas-v5 NetCDF, set TIDE_MODEL_DIR in .env to the unpacked directory. See Chapter 3.


B.2.5 pyTMD errors about “model not found”
Symptom: pyTMD.compute.tide_currents() raises FileNotFoundError: Model_TPXO9-atlas-v5_nc not found.
Root cause: One of the seven pyTMD 3.x quirks (Chapter 13). Most likely: TIDE_MODEL_DIR points at the model directory itself, but pyTMD wants its parent.
Fix: if your model is at ~/data/tpxo/TPXO9_atlas_v5/Model_h_M2_v5_nc, set TIDE_MODEL_DIR=~/data/tpxo/. pyTMD discovers the model from there.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.3 Simulation

B.3.1 “All seed points landed on land/NaN”
Symptom: RuntimeError: All seed points landed on land/NaN.
Root cause: Your seed disk is too close to or on top of land (very common in delta regions).
Fix: move the seed offshore. For Sundarbans:
python -m driftscope.simulate \
    --seed-lon 89.0 --seed-lat 20.8 --seed-radius 0.3
…or use --seed-mode bbox to fill the entire ocean portion of the bbox uniformly.


B.3.2 Particles all delete by day 3
Symptom: 500 particles seeded, 50 alive at day 3, 0 alive at day 10.
Root cause: The bbox is too small. Particles drift out of the domain and DeleteOOB removes them.
Fix: refetch with a wider bbox (~1.5× the typical drift distance: peak speed × runtime).


B.3.3 Simulation is suspiciously fast
Symptom: pset.execute() takes <1 second; trajectory file has 0 particles.
Root cause: All seed points landed on land in a way that run_simulation() didn’t catch (rare, but possible if the currents file’s land mask differs from our heuristic).
Fix: open the currents file and inspect:
ds = xr.open_dataset("...")
print(ds.uo.isel(time=0).count())  # should be > 0
If 0, your bbox is entirely land — fix the bbox.


B.3.4 parcels prints where='out' warning
Symptom: pages of UserWarning: 'where' used without 'out' from parcels’ particledata.py.
Root cause: parcels v3 + numpy 2.x deprecation. Library bug, not yours.
Fix: already filtered in simulate.py:19. If you see it, the filter was edited or numpy was bumped — update parcels (conda update parcels) or restore the filter.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.4 Plotting

B.4.1 Trajectory plot looks like a single line
Symptom: Plot shows what looks like one trajectory with 81 points, not 500 trajectories.
Root cause: Loading the wrong file, or only the first particle’s trajectory.
Fix: check the dataframe length:
df = traj_to_dataframe(ds)
print(df['traj'].nunique(), 'trajectories')
print(df['time'].nunique(), 'time steps')
print(len(df), 'rows')
500 × 81 should give 40,500 rows. If it gives 81, you’re loading wrong.


B.4.2 Map shows particles in wrong hemisphere
Symptom: trajectory plot shows points on the wrong continent.
Root cause: HYCOM uses 0..360 longitude convention internally and sometimes leaks through. Check if your particle longitudes are >180.
Fix: in the post-processing, normalize:
df['lon'] = ((df['lon'] + 180) % 360) - 180
The fetcher does this on save; user code that reads the trajectory zarr directly may need to redo it.


B.4.3 SST plot shows “300 K” colorbar
Symptom: temperature axis is in 280–310 K range.
Root cause: forgot to convert OSTIA from Kelvin to Celsius.
Fix: T_celsius = T_kelvin - 273.15 before plotting. The dynamics-snapshot script does this explicitly.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.5 Quarto book

B.5.1 quarto render fails with “command not found”
Symptom: bash: quarto: command not found.
Root cause: Quarto CLI not installed.
Fix: install from quarto.org/docs/get-started. Single binary, no Python dependencies. Smoke test:
quarto check


B.5.2 Code chunks fail to execute on render
Symptom: quarto render docs/ errors out on a {python} chunk.
Root cause: Quarto can’t find the right Python. By default it uses the system Python, which doesn’t have xarray, parcels, etc.
Fix: configure Quarto to use the conda env. Either:

conda activate driftscope before running quarto render.
Or set QUARTO_PYTHON env var to the env’s python:
export QUARTO_PYTHON=/path/to/miniconda/envs/driftscope/bin/python
quarto render docs/



B.5.3 Math symbols render as raw \dots
Symptom: Equations show \frac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt} instead of rendered math.
Root cause: KaTeX/MathJax not loading. Most likely your output is PDF and the LaTeX engine is missing.
Fix: for HTML output: ensure JavaScript is enabled in the browser; math should render via MathJax. For PDF: install LaTeX (tinytex is the easy option):
quarto install tinytex

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.6 Performance

B.6.1 Simulation runs out of memory
Symptom: Python killed by OOM, or “MemoryError” during pset.execute().
Root cause: Likely too many particles for the available RAM — each particle has a few-dozen-byte state, and trajectories are written to disk in chunks. 100k+ particles can be heavy.
Fix: reduce --particles. 500–2000 is the sweet spot for exploration; 10k+ is for production-grade ensembles.


B.6.2 Plots take forever to render
Symptom: df.plot() on the full trajectory dataframe sits.
Root cause: 40,000+ scatter points × matplotlib = slow.
Fix: subsample. df.sample(n=5000).plot(...) is plenty for visual inspection. For final plots, use 2D histogram (np.histogram2d → imshow) instead of scatter.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.7 When in doubt

Read the docstring of the function that’s misbehaving. Most gotchas are documented there.
git log -p path/to/file.py | head -100 — recent changes often reveal why a workaround exists.
Memory files in memory/ hold notes on past gotchas (especially the pyTMD ones).
scripts/ contain working end-to-end examples for every non-trivial use case. If you can’t get something to work, see if there’s a script that does it.

A mature Lagrangian-modeling workflow is 30% physics, 30% data plumbing, 20% bbox/grid bookkeeping, 20% troubleshooting. The first 30% is what’s interesting; the rest is what makes the first 30% reliable.
